items.body: By the third instalment of their Is Noise series, TAKAAT [pronounced tuh-cot and meaning “noise” in the Tuareg language Tamashek] have moved further from the raw collision of Tuareg guitar and punk that initially defined the project. The trio has become a duo here, without Souleymane Ibrahim’s live drums or any vocals. Vol. 3 is more exploratory and searching, less concerned with songs than with seeing how far Ahmoudou Madassane and Mikey Coltun can stretch their shared musical language. Drum machines, drones and field recordings move into the space left behind. The four-part Ijit N’elwan begins almost by withholding TAKAAT altogether. “Ijit N’elwan 1” opens with field recordings and remains a brief, ambient introduction, establishing a sense of place before amplification takes over. The second part strips things down to an extended, heavily distorted guitar passage whose sustained tones eventually push the track into drone territory. “Ijit N’elwan 3” initially reveals something bluesier in Madassane’s playing, but gradually acquires greater weight and distortion as it progresses, while the final part heads somewhere more psychedelic. Coltun’s comments in the accompanying interview help explain why this expansion feels natural. He draws a connection between the trance-like repetition at the heart of Tuareg guitar music and drone, as well as between the distortion of contemporary Takamba—music blasted through overloaded radios and megaphone speakers—and the punk, noise and experimental music that shaped his own listening. On Vol. 3, those affinities no longer need to be announced: they have become part of the music’s vocabulary. There is also a deliberate sense of risk. Each new TAKAAT EP enters a different world while remaining recognisably part of the same universe, and Vol. 3 takes that idea further than its predecessors. The duo format makes the music feel simultaneously more exposed and more open-ended as well as restless and unafraid of charting new territory. To make sense of the noise we reached out directly to TAKAAT with Mikey Coltun answering our questions. Across the three Is Noise volumes, TAKAAT has moved quite quickly from the raw Tuareg guitar and punk energy of Vol. 1, through the live-to-tape Tinariwen reworkings of Vol. 2, to the drones, drum machines, field recordings and much denser noise of Vol. 3. Was this evolution something you imagined when TAKAAT began, or has each volume simply opened up possibilities for the next one? Mikey Coltun: It’s been a mix of both. We knew there was a lot to explore sonically when Ahmoudou and I started the band but to what extent was a bit more unknown until we started touring and experimenting both live and during the recording process. Each Is Noise is recorded to tape. That’s kinda the overall concept. Similarly if you look at the album art (shout out to our designer Can Misirlioglu) throughout the volumes the structure remains the same but is a different perspective and zoomed out throughout each volume. This was intentional from the beginning as it relates to the music and the progression of each Is Noise volume. Mikey, you’ve drawn a connection between the distortion of modern Takamba—particularly the tehardent amplified through blown-out radios—and the noise and experimental music you grew up with in Washington, D.C. [Andy Downing, Matter News, 4 March 2026]. On Vol. 3, do those traditions actually meet in the way you make sound, or are they still distinct references that you bring into TAKAAT from different directions? Mikey Coltun: There’s definitely all of those influences – Takamba, punk, noise and experimental music present on Vol. 3. Similar to later era John Coltrane, a lot of Tuareg music is drone music at its core. With Tuareg guitar music, a simple chord structure with trance-like rhythms and melodies often played for long periods of time is no different than the spirituality of drone music and this is something Ahmoudou and I were interested in exploring. Taking our guitar and bass and blasting it through amps creating different sonic distortions can be also heard when seeing Takamba music live but instead of the guitar amps you have a blown out radio receiver roaring through megaphone speakers. As Ahmoudou has put it, TAKAAT is the “feeling of being in the desert at night.” Vol. 3 also changes the basic instrumental architecture of TAKAAT: drum machines, drone synths and manipulated field recordings become central alongside Ahmoudou’s guitar and Mikey’s bass. What interested you about moving away from the more recognisable guitar/bass/drums setup of the earlier volumes, and how did that change the way you approached improvisation? Mikey Coltun: It’s important for Ahmoudou and I to be experimenting musically and taking risks. We talk a lot about how Taureg legends Tinariwen pushed, what Tuareg music is, and what we’re doing with TAKAAT is breaking the expectations of the known Tuareg rock sound. We want each record to push into a different world while still staying in the universe of TAKAAT. This goes the same with our shows. Each tour Ahmoudou and I want to present something different with TAKAAT. The first few tours we did the trio, last tour was a duo presenting a loud drone and blown out drum machines, and next tour will be something different too. We’re taking risks and we want people to come take these risks with us. This is the only way to push out of comfort zones and create something new. You’ve described the trust developed through eight years of playing together as something that allows TAKAAT to take risks, while Mikey has also spoken about the project as a return to a more DIY world where there is less pressure to perform in a particular way [Andy Downing, Matter News, 4 March 2026]. Does TAKAAT give you a kind of freedom that you don’t necessarily have in Mdou Moctar—and has that freedom changed the way you listen and respond to one another when you play? Mikey Coltun: It was really clear early on touring together with Mdou Moctar that Ahmoudou and I were excited by similar music. I brought a lot of different types of bands on tour with Mdou. All of the music is by groups and artists that I love. While some of the groups could have been challenging to listeners it was important to me to draw that connection with what we were doing with Mdou. Mdou’s music was different and challenging to some in the Tuareg wedding scene in Agadez, Niger. With a lot of these bands I brought on tour I found Ahmoudou’s interest peaked. Whenever there was an opportunity on tour I would take him to see sound installations, free jazz groups, modern art, etc… and he really does appreciate that. Because Ahmoudou and I have similar interests sonically, there is a lot of trust and comfortability to experiment and try new things together with TAKAAT. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: experimental / Tuareg guitar / drone / noise / psychedelic
items._cn_summary: TAKAAT的第三张《Is Noise》系列专辑进一步脱离了图阿雷吉他与朋克的原始碰撞，转向更加探索性的声音实验。由双人组合呈现，鼓机、无人机和田野录音取代了现场鼓与人声，占据了更大的空间。四段式的《Ijit N'elwan》从环境化的开场逐步引入失真吉他长音，滑入无人机领域，随后展现蓝调色彩与迷幻氛围的交替。专辑延续了每卷录音至磁带的整体概念，成员Mikey Coltun解释了图阿雷吉他音乐中恍惚式重复与无人机美学之间的内在联系，以及传统Takamba音乐中通过过载收音机和扩音器播放所产生的失真质感——这些元素已自然地融入作品的词汇表，不再需要刻意声明。整体呈现出暴露感与开放性并存的特质，在熟悉与陌生之间不断游走。

items.body: Thematically, Post Dub Cities hearkens back to Future Sound of London’s Dead Cities, while tonally it recalls Murcof’s Rememberanza. Adriano Zanni‘s vision of a future world is the cold reflection of a present reality in which many places are already deserted: peeling houses, dilapidated storefronts, bombed villages. At one time, they teemed with life. Once humans have no more use for a city, they abandon it, leaving only rubble and questionable specters. The reasons may be as far afield as the loss of jobs, the evaporation of resources, or a campaign of bombs. More than anything, Post Dub Cities is an album of mood. Zanni wants his listeners to be uncomfortable, to regard these cities as one does the stone wreckage of Ozymandius. From the opening notes of “Crisopoli” (also the first single), he casts a spell of resignation and despair. The pace is slow, but not sluggish; the beats restrained, but not soft. Someone has to bear witness. In “Pyramiden,” the tone grows harsher, with amplified whispers, clacking pipes and cavernous echoes. Were it not for the dub timbres, one might call this industrial or post-industrial music. Each piece seems to hide another piece behind it: a subdued rhythm, a moving shadow. In “Centralia,” sharp beats stumble like scavengers sifting through wreckage. These visitors may not be human, or even humanoid; in Alan Weisman’s classic The World Without Us, everything from roaches to raccoons reclaims its own. Rust abrades metal; girders bend; branches break through glass. The accompanying pdf is essential to the release. Referencing Calvino and Marcelli, Zanni writes of the empty city as an “echo chamber,” an image reflected in the music. A hundred pages of sublime black and white photographs follow, captured in cities around the world over the past two decades. The unifying feature is the lack of any human presence, as if scrubbed from existence (insert sci-fi theory here). Proof of humanity’s presence remains, but without context. In Zanni’s own words: “memory without recollection, structure without use, body without inhabitants.” In response, the music is architectural: one imagines a grid in which beats and notes are purposely placed. Belgrade, Vienna, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Dublin, Sarajevo, Rome, London, Prague, Madrid, Krakow, Istanbul, Lisbon, Palermo and more, all deserted: buildings empty, rollercoasters stilled, markets abandoned, art left to dissolve. Not a single vehicle is visible, even on the highway. One can see what humans have done, but not where they have gone. In what seems to be the final image, a massive wall of chairs is ready for a group of patrons who never arrive. Capturing these images must have required remarkable patience and timing. The last bonus track, “San Zhi Pod City,” offers a surprise: the appearance of a human voice. Even this turns out to be a loop, a remnant, an echo. But Zanni does have a final trick up his sleeve: on page 99, the people reappear, filling the square. The last four images show humanity wall to literal wall: perhaps too much humanity, suggesting a reason for its removal or demise. As much as one pores through “Kadykchan” and “San Zhi Pod City” for a matching restoration, one cannot hear it in the grooves. The listener is left to ponder whether the detritus of humanity might hold any intrinsic value, or if it is only sound and fury, signifying nothing. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: dub / post-industrial / dark ambient / experimental electronic
items._cn_summary: Adriano Zanni 的《Post Dub Cities》以"后废墟"为概念框架，将声音景观与城市空无进行跨媒介结合。专辑附带一本数百页的黑白摄影集，拍摄自贝尔格莱德、维也纳、巴塞罗那、萨拉热窝、伊斯坦布尔等全球城市，所有画面均无人类痕迹。音乐层面以dub音色为骨架，节奏缓慢但具推进力，合成器与回响空间营造出压迫与疏离感。"Pyramiden"中放大的低语与管腔回响接近工业质感，"Centralia"的破碎节拍如拾荒者在残骸中翻找。配乐附带的PDF文本引用卡尔维诺与马尔塞利，将空城描述为"回声室"，与音乐本身形成互文。终曲"San Zhi Pod City"中突然出现的人声实为循环采样，暗示人类本身已成为废墟中的回声残留。

items.body: In a house in Lomé, a woman kept a set of ceremonial pots she used for preparing potions for the older women of the Vodun temples. Vodun is the West African religion the Ewe and Fon have practised across Togo and Benin for centuries, the one that crossed the Atlantic on slave ships and became Haitian Vodou and Louisiana Voodoo. Its spirits are bound up with natural forces and they are reached through drumming and singing, so those women sang constantly. Her grandson grew up believing all that singing had gone into the clay and stayed there. Years later he took the pots and built a drum kit out of them. His name is Toto Tchilatchi, and half of what Nana Benz du Togo carry onto a stage is those pots. The other half is a bass David Kasanku built out of PVC drainpipe. He used to play bass, then spent four years assembling the gazé tuyau. Once it went underneath Toto’s kit, the pots and drums came to life, and together they made a groove full of sub-bass and complex polyrhythms. That groove became the bedrock for three singers, Lady Apoc, Parus Kekeli and Izealedu, with a small vintage Korg keyboard alongside their voices. The band’s word for what all of it adds up to is trance. They describe Vodun itself as being about rhythm, trance, nature and connection, and Lady Apoc says theirs comes from “repetitive energy.“ None of the five knew each other until 2019, when Peter Solo, the leader of Vaudou Game, came to Lomé to run a workshop and brought local musicians and artists together for it. Out of that workshop came the band, and Solo has produced them ever since. They took their name from the Nana Benz, the wax-print traders of Lomé’s central market who drove Mercedes-Benz cars and were confided in by the powerful. The band say they admire the courage and force those women showed in patriarchal societies. They sing in English, French and Mina, over the Vodun scales of the snake, Dan, and of Mami Wata, about women and the earth, and they say protecting one is inseparable from protecting the other. Their feminism, the band say, comes from the strength and resilience of African women, and their ecology from Vodun itself, and they say protecting women and protecting the earth cannot be pulled apart. Like many people of their generation, they grew up with mixed feelings about Vodun and were taught to be ashamed of parts of it, and at some point they moved away from it. Going back gave them their voice back. They stopped trying to fit into a musical category and started creating from who they are. Even so, they never set out to put Vodun in the spotlight, and years of work in the shadows came before they dared to get on a stage. Their first concert in Europe was Transmusicales de Rennes in 2022, and AGO followed the year after, recorded at the OTODI studio in Lomé with Solo producing. They went back to OTODI in December 2024 to record SÉ NAM, again with Solo, and it came out in June 2025. Its eleven tracks have a more contemporary production and more room for groove and rhythm. The title means “understand me” in Mina, one of the three languages they sing in. In October they bring it to WOMEX in Las Palmas… For this episode of Musical Road to WOMEX they answered our questions about how Vodun meets the dancefloor, what their handmade instruments do and what they hope to find on the island: they want to hear the timple, meet local musicians and find out what traces of African and Atlantic exchange can still be heard in Canarian music, and they arrive, as they put it, with their ears open. The playlist at the end lets you hear what they are bringing. You’ve been described as pioneers of “digital voodoo”. For someone hearing you for the first time, how would you introduce the meeting of Vodun tradition and the dancefloor? For us, Digital Vodou is not about taking something old and trying to make it modern. It is about showing that Vodun is already alive and has always had the power to evolve. Vodun is about rhythm, trance, nature and connection. And the dancefloor can be a place for that too. People come together, move together, let go. We bring traditional rhythms, songs, percussion and the handmade instruments we create into electronic music, bass and contemporary sounds. For us, it is a meeting between something very old and something that is still being born. That is what makes it feel both ancestral and futuristic. The band takes its name from the Nana Benz, the market women who turned the wax-print trade into power and independence. What did diving back into your Vodun heritage, after leaving it behind, open up for you musically? It gave us our voice back. Like many people from our generation, we grew up with mixed feelings about Vodun. There were things we were taught to be ashamed of, so at some point we moved away from it. Coming back to it changed the way we saw ourselves. We realised that Vodun is not only a spiritual tradition. It is also a way of understanding our relationship with the earth, with women, with our ancestors and with each other. And musically, it opened a whole world for us: rhythms, melodies, stories, symbols. Things that were already inside us. We stopped trying to fit into a musical category. We started creating from who we really are. WOMEX lands this year in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, an Atlantic island whose own traditions ride on the timple, a five-string guitar that carries both African and Latin American trade routes. What are you most curious to discover there? We are curious about the connections between the different traditions. Islands are special places. Cultures arrive there, meet, change and survive. We want to hear the timple, meet local musicians and discover what traces of African and Atlantic exchanges can still be heard in Canarian music. And honestly, we are excited about the unexpected. Maybe one of our handmade instruments will meet a sound from the island in a way we never imagined. That is what we love about music. Your instruments are handmade and upcycled, the gazé tuyaux among them, and your themes are feminist and ecological. In a WOMEX programme full of traditions, what makes your sound and your message unmistakably yours? For us, everything is connected. The recycled instruments are not just something you see on stage. They are part of our sound and part of the way we think. We take things that people throw away and give them another life. In a way, we do the same with our stories and traditions. We take things that have been misunderstood or pushed aside and bring them back into the present. Our feminism comes from the strength and resilience of African women. And our connection to ecology comes from Vodun itself. We often say, “Whoever does not respect women does not respect nature.” For us, that says a lot about who Nana Benz Du Togo is. WOMEX is built on unexpected meetings. Which artists, labels or collaborators are you hoping to cross paths with in Las Palmas? We don’t really have a list of names. We want to meet people who are deeply connected to where they come from but are not afraid to experiment. Artists who can move between tradition, ritual, electronic music, performance and new ideas. And that is one of the things we love about WOMEX. You can have a conversation with someone backstage and suddenly discover that there is something you can create together. We are coming with our ears open. You’ve toured Europe and built a reputation as a live force. Does a room of delegates and music professionals change how you bring the trance and the groove of your set? Not really. Of course, we know that WOMEX is important and that there will be a lot of professionals in the room. But once we are on stage, we have to be ourselves. Whether there are one hundred people, a thousand people or music professionals watching us, we want the same thing: for people to feel the music in their bodies. We want them to forget for a moment who they are supposed to be and simply become part of the rhythm. That is when the magic happens. “Voodoo is Nature,” you’ve said. Gran Canaria is a volcanic island shaped by the ocean around it. Does a landscape like that speak to the ecology at the heart of your songs? Absolutely. When you see a volcanic landscape, you are reminded that the earth is alive. It is powerful, it changes, it moves. For us, nature is not something outside of us. In Vodun, it is a living presence. The ocean, the wind, the stone, the fire inside the earth, these are not just things around us. They are forces. So being on an island shaped by the ocean and volcanoes feels very familiar to our way of thinking. It reminds us that we are part of something much bigger than ourselves. Your work carries a clear message about women’s strength and respect for the planet. Is there something you feel especially compelled to say through this showcase? Yes. We want to remind people that protecting women and protecting the earth are not separate things. We believe our traditions can still teach us something about that balance. We are not trying to go back to the past. We are trying to understand what we can take from it to imagine a different future. For us, women are creators, transmitters, protectors and forces of transformation. That is something we want to celebrate through our music. After SÉ NAM, what’s next? New recordings, new collaborations, directions you’re keen to push the project toward? SÉ NAM was an important chapter for us, but we already feel the next one coming. We are working on new music and pushing the dialogue between ritual percussion, the instruments we make ourselves and electronic production even further. We also want to work with artists from other parts of Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America. There are so many shared histories, rhythms and spiritual connections across the Atlantic that we would love to explore. We want to keep moving forward without losing our roots. If you could write a personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and discover your showcase, what would it say? Come with your body before your expectations. Come to dance, listen, feel and maybe remember something older than all of us. We are bringing rhythms from Togo, women’s voices, handmade instruments and the energy of Digital Vodou. Don’t just come and watch us. Come and experience it with us. If you join us, we will create the ceremony together.   On 23 October at the Plaza Stage in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Nana Benz du Togo will ask the WOMEX crowd to forget for a moment who they are supposed to be and become part of the rhythm   PLAYLIST: NANA BENZ DU TOGO X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Nana Benz du Togo appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: 这支来自多哥的乐队将沃顿宗教仪式的精神内核转化为舞台表演，核心乐器极为独特：鼓手Toto Tchilatchi用祖母留下的沃顿仪式陶罐自制了一套鼓组，贝斯手David Kasanku则用四年时间以PVC排水管制作了一支低音号角乐器"gazé tuyau"。陶罐鼓与管乐器构成了低音与复杂复节奏的基座，三位歌手（Lady Apoc、Parus Kekeli、Izealedu）配合一台老式Korg键盘，在英语、法语与Mina语中演唱蛇神Dan和Mami Wata的沃顿音阶。乐队2019年由Vaudou Game主脑Peter Solo在洛美工作坊中组建，融合女性赋权与生态保护主题，2025年专辑《SÉ NAM》在洛美OTODI工作室录制完成。

items.body: John Coltrane – Live at the Village Vanguard (Impulse, 1997) By Kenneth Blanchard There are certain recordings that stretched my grasp of jazz (and indeed music). Andrew Hill’s Point of Departure comes to mind. Coltrane’s LVV collection is another. Recorded over four nights in 1961 at the Jerusalem of Jazz, only five of the originally recorded numbers were released in the following two years. The 1997 box set is a genuine treasure. The structure of the music remains within standard hop bop spaces, but the moods blossom into an entirely new ecosystem. The inclusion of Eric Dolphy was one of Trane’s most brilliant moves. On Naima, Spiritual, India , his low horns (also sax and bass clarinet) perfectly match Trane’s tenor and soprano sax. Trane’s interest in alternative spiritual and musical traditions is obvious enough. His famous “sheets of sound” slide in and out of every line. I find the articulation of Coltrane’s own personality to be as vivid here as on any of his recordings. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / hard bop / spiritual jazz / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 这张合集收录了1961年在爵士圣地Village Vanguard连续四个夜晚的现场录音，五年后以盒装形式完整呈现。演出虽扎根于硬波普的和声结构，但情绪与精神维度已延伸至一个全新的音乐生态系统。Eric Dolphy的加入是关键一笔，他使用低音单簧管、阿尔托萨克斯及巴松管，与Coltrane的次中音和高音萨克斯形成罕见的低音声部对话，在《Naima》《Spiritual》《India》等曲目中构建出东西方精神传统交织的声场。Coltrane标志性的"音幕"技法贯穿每一条乐句的进出，演奏高度即兴化与个性化，是其生涯中性格表达最鲜明的现场录音之一。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — In the early 1980s, German musician Peter Frohmader, creator of the famous Nekropolis trilogy, teamed up with none other than Artemiy Artemiev. Like Frohmader, Artemiev was an electronic musician, but he was also the son of Eduard Artemiev, a pioneer of Russian electronic music who had composed, among other works, the soundtrack for Andrei Tarkovsky's film Solaris.Here, each playing a synthesizer, they weave a subtle sonic tapestry; utilizing electric guitar, bass, and gong percussion, Frohmader shapes a progressive symphony that evokes the "space rock" era of Pink Floyd, the psychedelia of the band Gong, and the harmonic style of Klaus Schulze. What makes the work novel and original is the way guitar variations play against synthesizer loops, much like an overcast sky filled with countless clouds, where rays of light occasionally break through the monochromatic sheen, tearing the canvas here and there to complete the panorama. Hints of rock and blues emerge, improvisations set against the unwavering electronic foundations, creating a truly unique texture.Later on, it takes on a percussive intensity as the guitar launches into psychedelic jams, almost as if Steve Hillage had stepped onto the scene, and the term "electronic progressive rock" acquires a new meaning; the fusion becomes even more deeply intertwined in "Space Icon." "Mir" is the second track; in Russian, it means "Peace," but it can also signify "Universe" or "World." This double meaning, this duality, suits the track's music perfectly; in contrast to the expansive opening, the sound is relaxed, mysterious, and introspective. Electronic music evokes sensations and moods that are not always associated with words, at least not initially, yet it is that secondary level of meaning that we are attempting to explore here.Once again, layered synthesizers and gongs serve an ethereal melody that seems to evoke the presence of a hidden soprano, while "Channeling", the third track, is more tribal, primitive, organic, and minimalist; it calls to mind the East and reminded me of Brand X's percussion, as Frohmader actually plays fretless bass on this track. Turning to the East, "Zen Garden" fully immerses us in that realm; one can picture Pierre Moerlen and his percussion work with Gong, yet set within a context where everything seems to float. The synthesizers resemble currents of wind, and simultaneously pan flutes, reinforcing a sense of earthly connection. "Space Icon" orbits between these two poles: the earthly realm and the space beyond Earth."Cosmic Jungle" is an expansive closing track that fuses the jungle and the cosmos; it gradually becomes saturated with dissonance as the sounds of birds morph into tribal drums, contrasting sharply with those distinctly electric dissonances, before circling back to the minimalism of the opening, ultimately concluding with an ambient finish reminiscent of Delia Derbyshire and the Standard Music Library.Recorded between Art Recording Studio in Moscow and Studio Nekropolis in Munich, this collaborative album culminates in a projection of Russo-German influences that stands as an icon of that very fusion.
items._genre: progressive electronic / space music / experimental ambient
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是德国音乐人Peter Frohmader与俄罗斯电子音乐先驱Artemiy Artemiev的合作成果，两人在合成器框架下编织层次丰富的音景。吉他即兴段落与合成器循环交织碰撞，形成独特质感：迷幻的吉他独奏在电子底色上展开，类似Steve Hillage式的psichedelic jam；加入电贝斯、锣等打击乐器后，作品呈现出部落感和东方色彩。标题曲在太空感与大地感两极之间游走，后半段逐渐走向不协和与张力，鸟鸣声渐变为部落鼓点，最终回归简约并以氛围音色收尾。整张作品融合了Pink Floyd式的空间感、Gong的迷幻律动以及Klaus Schulze的和声语言，将电子前卫摇滚拓展为一种新的表达范式。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Right off the bat, playing the harmonium like a classical piano hints at the atypical nature of this album. Five Suns is like an explosion containing multiple explosions within itself, much like fireworks that conceal other pyrotechnics, releasing them at just the right moment. Guitar and organ flesh out the trio's sound, which surges forward with the Mellotron in Part 2 of the Five Suns suite.We are talking about the English band Guapo; they constantly shift and mutate, yet their musical vision remains consistently compelling and challenging, both for the musicians themselves and for the listener. Perhaps therein lies the secret: while their previous album, Great Sage, Equal of Heaven, was a duo featuring a guest saxophonist, here, as a stripped-down trio, they sound richer and darker. They evoke a King Crimson-esque vibe infused with dissonant jazz-rock, while also bringing to mind the dense fusion of the Norwegian band Red Kite and the psychedelic space rock of Monomith.The fact that both Matt Thompson and Daniel O'Sullivan alternated between guitar and samplers, while Dave Smith varied the drum rhythms, contributed to the suite's unpredictability. This was followed by subtle moments of counterpoint between the bass and the Rhodes, which in turn served as a foundation for new drum solos; the drums never stood alone for long, however, before the guitar rejoined the mix. Just when the balance seemed to tip toward Mahavishnu-style fusion, that compulsion for avant-garde composition returned, defining the entirety of Part 3 of Five Suns, as dissonance and psychedelia took center stage.Another key point for me was their ability to know exactly when to break up repetitive sections with rhythm changes; every element had its own purpose and appeared at precisely the right moment. There is room for groove in Five Suns, just as at other moments chaos takes over and things spiral out of control, a chaos that ultimately proves to be controlled, much like improvisation in classic jazz, a passage that highlights precisely the strength of the other."Five Suns," Part 4, with its more prominent organ and contrapuntal drumming, sounds more progressive and thrilling, building to a near-dramatic climax reminiscent of Yndi Halda's Enjoy Eternal Bliss. The fifth and final part carries an aura of danger and suspense; as the distorted guitar gives way to the keyboards, the music plunges into the void of an organ solo lost in an unfathomable abyss."Mictlan" possesses the freshness, lightness, and fluidity of a unique piece, as if casting off the heavy burden of belonging to such a dense suite; the Rhodes floats freely, and the drums follow suit in an exercise that is as playful as it is anarchic. Here, the Mellotron reigns supreme alongside the distorted bass, representing the "rock 'n' roll" side of Guapo's avant-garde jazz-rock, while the music vibrates and sways, accelerating to perfectly complement what stands as the flip side of Five Suns. It wouldn't be complete without the other side of the coin, "Topan", where they deconstruct fusion in the style of Eskaton, with their degraded harmonies, only to end with the same mystery with which we began: an open-ended conclusion that serves as the best guarantee of an imminent return.
items._cn_summary: 这是英国乐队Guapo在2004年发行的前卫专辑，以三重奏编制探索了极为密集的实验性声音景观。乐队在键盘、口琴、吉他与采样器之间不断切换，鼓手则以多变的节奏型态支撑全篇结构。专辑以一首长达多个乐章的《Five Suns》套曲为核心，结合了King Crimson式的不协和爵士摇滚、挪威乐队Red Kite式的密集融合，以及迷幻空间摇滚的元素。乐队擅长在重复段落中适时插入节奏突变，制造出介于控制与混沌之间的张力。末段加入的Mellotron为整体增添了丰富的复古前卫质感。Mictlan一曲则以Rhodes键盘的轻灵与鼓点的顽皮形成对比，展现出乐队在繁复之外的流动性。整体呈现了高度自觉的结构意识与强烈的实验冲动。

items.excerpt: While much of Grisha Shakhnes’ music could be categorised as obscure and undifferentiated, “The distance between a word and a deed” strikes me as perhaps his most elusive effort yet. items.body: While much of Grisha Shakhnes’ music could be categorised as obscure and undifferentiated, “The distance between a word and a deed” strikes me as perhaps his most elusive effort yet. (It’s also his longest, clocking in at around two hours if you count the bonus material included with the download.) This elusiveness makes me think of the monochrome paintings of artists such as Robert Rauschenberg and Ad Reinhardt — blank and featureless at first glance, but on closer inspection a subtle wealth of detail emerges from the traces of brushstrokes or the uneven application of paint. Shakhnes’ music has such hidden details too: the long, terrifying crescendo in ‘Stockholm variation #2.5’ and the quiet opening to ‘Stockholm variation #3’ are two of the more prominent examples. Indeed, after multiple listens the various whoops, rumbles, crackles, whistles, and distortions heard across the album could hardly be called ‘undifferentiated’ in any strict sense, but what is interesting is that the sense of blankness and elusiveness remains, even after the details have become audible. It’s as if the album invited (at least) two equally valid and rewarding ways of listening: you can zoom in on the subtle nuances and changing timbres, or you can let the quietly thundering, rattling flow carry you away from all concepts and all thought. In the latter mode, the music acts on the senses like a heavy downpour or the constant chugging of a train. Both ways of listening are rewarding, and can be switched between at will. Yet however one listens, there’s a vague sense of melancholy or restlessness that hangs in the air like a mist, preventing things from becoming too comfortable. This is not some kind of ganzfeld effect, creating a uniform stimulation field to trick the senses; rather, there’s the perception (hallucination?) of a certain turning away, a declining to comment, a silence that is allowed to fall behind and between the rumble and clatter. Sometimes the distance between a word and a deed can be very great. the distance between a word and a deed by Grisha Shakhnes Grisha Shakhnes / Disappearing Records
items._cn_summary: Grisha Shakhnes的专辑呈现出极为模糊且难以捉摸的聆听体验，全长约两小时。乐评将其比作罗伯特·劳森伯格和阿德·莱因哈特式的单色绘画，乍听之下平淡无特征，但细听后涌出丰富的声响层次与细微变化。专辑中存在两种并行的聆听方式：可以聚焦于作品中细微的音色变化、长时值的恐怖渐强以及各种声响事件，也可以在低沉轰鸣与咔嗒声中让意识脱离概念漂移。评论强调，尽管细节逐渐浮现，整体的空白感与不可捉摸性始终保持。音乐中弥漫着一种模糊的忧郁与不安，如同大雾般阻止听者进入完全舒适的状态，但并非通过均质化刺激来欺骗感官。专辑留有大段沉默与拒绝表态的空间，标题所暗示的言与行之间的距离在音乐结构中持续延展。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.
items.label: Artist release
items._genre: folk classical fusion / Slovak traditional music / chamber ensemble / contemporary composition
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由小提琴家Ján Kružliak Jr.主导，核心思路是将斯洛伐克传统民间音乐与其古典音乐传统重新连接。曲目大多改编自斯洛伐克作曲家Eugen Suchoň、Ilja Zeljenka、Alexander Moyzes以及深入斯洛伐克采集民间音乐的匈牙利作曲家巴托克。演奏由三个团体协作完成：Kružliak领导的Spectrum弦乐四重奏、传统风格的Nogaband乐队，以及女声团体Ulijanky。每首作品都标注了采风来源的村庄与乐人，编曲既保留了古典作曲的技法框架，又植入了民间演奏的原始力度与人声质感，乐评特别强调其粗粝、有生命力的特质，区别于管弦乐化的平滑处理。这是一份将学院派作曲资源与乡村音乐根脉双向打通的有意义的尝试。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._genre: experimental / folktronica / African traditional fusion / electronic
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters发行，是德国出生、驻扎肯尼亚的打击乐手Sven Kacirek与卢欧族歌手Ogoya Nengo及Odi Ratengo的首次三重合作。83岁的Nengo带来肯尼亚东部传统dodo歌唱，与搭档Ratengo形成人声呼应。Kacirek则以Buchla合成器、手打打击乐与套鼓构建电子节奏层，电子纹理在曲目中以近乎不可察觉的方式逐渐浮现，最终与声乐融为一体，使根源传统获得前卫色彩。评论指出，这种真正全球化的跨文化协作既扎根于非洲本土传统，又拥抱电子与实验手段，让根源成为先锋，让创新仿佛延续千年。整体制作强调声音层叠的微妙渐进与人声与电子的平衡张力。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion

Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items._genre: avant-garde / experimental / contemporary classical / ambient / progressive
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz与意大利作曲家Paladino及诗人Ferrari合作专辑《Songs of Compassion》收录十一首歌曲，将钢琴、弦乐、木管与合成器音景编织成非线性、模态化的声响结构，突破西方和声运动的惯性思维。评论将其比作Steve Reich与Philip Glass式的极简重复脉络，而非传统摇滚乐。Moskowitz的演唱如同训练有素的方法派演员，以世界疲惫而智慧的声音承载哲学化歌词，旋律随意识流动而非遵循功能和声逻辑。歌词延续1960年代抗议歌曲传统，从《Pale Wanderer》对威权主义共谋的剖析，到《Charlottesville》直面新纳粹集会，兼顾时政批判与对死亡、人类在宇宙中位置的冥想。这是一张融合先锋作曲、诗化歌词与政治意识的跨界作品，由意大利小厂牌Silentes发行。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 的第二张专辑以手工自制乐器为核心，所有声音均来自废料与日常物品拼装的独特乐器，包括 tassofons、kitchenofon 等。乐评特别指出这些自制乐器在录音棚环境下依然音准准确、音色丰富。曲目融合克莱兹默、昆比亚、非洲节拍、桑巴、中东旋律等多种世界音乐元素，每首作品对应一种文化风格，即兴段落展现扎实的演奏功底。标题曲以木块、沙锤、响板构建 Afrobeat 律动，配以马林巴与铃铛装饰的旋律线。整张专辑体现了将垃圾转化为音乐媒介的创作理念，跨越文化边界展现音乐普遍性，手工乐器的实验性与世界音乐融合形成独特听感。

items.body: In August of this year, New Focus Recordings released New Music for Two Voices, an impressive collection of acapella vocal music by sopranos Susan Narucki and Kirsten Ashley Wiest. This lavish album features a full hour masterful singing of six contemporary works, including three world premiere recordings. Susan Narucki is an accomplished soprano who has appeared as a soloist with the Cleveland Orchestra, Los Angeles Philharmonic, the San Francisco Symphony, among many other international appearances. She is presently on the faculty of the Department of Music at UC San Diego. Kirsten Ashley Wiest is an award-winning coloratura soprano who has performed and recorded alongside numerous GRAMMY winners, the Los Angeles Philharmonic, San Diego Symphony, Bang on a Can All-Stars and the Partch ensemble, among many others. Kirsten currently teaches voice at San Bernardino Valley College and University of California Riverside, New Music for Two Voices is a deep dive into the cutting edge of virtuoso vocal technique as it intersects with contemporary musical composition. The album is accompanied by excellent liner notes, full translations of the texts and biographical notes on the composers and the performers. The outstanding sound engineering is by Andrew Munsey and Kristina Tran. The first track on the album is come sempre (2025), by Dutch composer Rozalie Hirs. Although written just last year, the liner notes inform that this piece “…evokes music of an earlier time, with shifting tonal centers and interwoven melodic lines..” Running at over 7 minutes, it is one of the longer works of the entire album and is a world premiere. come sempre features two voices singing separately in Italian, sometimes together and sometimes in a call and response pattern. The vocal lines are often independent and weave in and around each other seamlessly in a series of lovely harmonies. There is no accompaniment anywhere in this album so the two singers must rely on their internal sense of rhythm and pitch. Where crisp phrases are present, these are always clean and punchy. Nothing ragged or blurry here; the notes are precise and balanced. As the piece proceeds it gradually increases in complexity, summoning ever greater technique. The singing by these two confident voices, however, is always controlled throughout. The poems of El trino persistente by Javier Tafur González are the inspiration for TRINOS, a series of twelve miniature works by Colombian composer Alba Potes. Commissioned by Susan Narucki in 2024, all are less than one minute long, yet these pieces sparkle like brilliant gems. The liner notes state that “Each of the twelve settings seems to capture a moment in time—by turns, lyrical, nostalgic, jubilant, hopeful.” “TRINOS: I. Jazmin” is the first of the twelve pieces and although less than a minute in length, it sets the standard for the precision and vocal technique that is heard throughout the entire work. A high vocal tone opens, then falls rapidly in pitch as a second voice joins in a middle register with dissonance. The singers must rely on their own intuition for pitch and timing – there are no accompanying chords or common rhythms. The overall feeling is one of welcome and portent. Although less than a minute in length, this first piece sets a high bar for vocal artistry. Other pieces in the work are similarly concise and illustrate the consistent level of virtuosity brought to bear by Wiest and Narucki. “TRINOS: II. Entra illuminando la casa”, at just 32 seconds in length ,is intense, with many jumps and leaps in the two voices. It shines like a fiery jewel. “TRINOS: IV. No saldré” features a middle register voice together with a lower voice in close harmony. Stretches of unusual dissonances challenge the singers, but are navigated successfully. “TRINOS: VI. Timida flor” opens with a strong voice soaring up very high with impressive power and good control. “TRINOS: VII. Ven, anclemos” is soft, with almost mournful feeling and quietly sentimental. The text, even in English translation, is perfect: “Come, let us anchor now hands entwined.” “TRINOS: IX. Se hundió el buque” by contrast, is completely different. A quiet, solo voice is heard in a middle register, reserved and subdued. The lyrics are more spoken than sung, producing a purposeful and deliberate sensibility. “TRINOS: XI. Podemos estar juntos” is another solo piece with a strong voice crying out as if in sadness. The singing here is expressive, yet delivered with great clarity. The final piece in the work is “TRINOS: XII. En los hilos”, a duet with the lower voice in sustained tones underneath a soaring, coloratura voice. The dissonances in the harmonies add a powerful, melancholy feeling to this. TRINOS is a masterful collection of small pieces that each deliver an emotional punch from the virtuosity of the performers. The third work on the album is From the Grammar of Dreams (1988), by Kaija Saariaho and consists of five pieces based on two separate texts from the American poet Sylvia Plath. The liner notes tell us that “The five duets demonstrate Saariaho’s unique compositional language, with its attention to fine gradations of vocal color, intricacy and flexibility of gesture, and a nearly overwhelming range of emotional expression.” The first duet, labeled simply “I”, opens with strange and painful sounds in the lower voice with struggling vocals in the second voice as if forcing out the words and notes. Leaps and jumps are heard in the upper voice accompanied by sustained and plaintive sounds from the lower. Just a little over 2 minutes long, this piece is expressively weird and haunting.“II”, the second piece in From the Grammar of Dreams begins with two sets of spoken words heard simultaneously. This is somewhat chaotic as there is no common tones or phrasing. One voice includes some rather gruesome details, as if recounting a nightmare. The voices are alternately speaking and singing and often very agitated. The music is complex and dynamic, yet confidently delivered. The third duet, “III” is soft and melodic; completely different in character from the previous pieces. There is lovely harmony in the two voices with lots of sustained notes and dramatic gestures. There is a welcome and mysterious feeling to this. “IV” opens with scratchy, breathy sounds followed by strong vocal music. The voices jump and soar as each part bounces breathlessly off the other. The two voices devolve in a sort of shouting match just before the piece concludes with a few short breaths. Amazing technique here. The final duet, “V”, begins with a series of sustained notes in both voices sung in a high register with prominent vibrato. The sounds loop around each other independently in pitch and dynamic. This produces an eerie feeling at times but is mostly strongly declarative. The fourth work on the album is NauðaR Níu [The Nine Needs] (2025), by Jeffrey Holmes. This collection of nine pieces is based on old Norse Runic carvings (ca. 5th through 12th century), as compiled and translated by the composer. As with the other works in this album, each piece is short, ranging from 37 seconds to a little over three and a half minutes. As explained in the liner notes, NauðaR Níu features some unusual accompaniment: “Throughout, the vocalists play a variety of percussion instruments; the sound of metal, skin, wood and natural materials contributing to the sense of a vast primeval landscape.” The opening piece of NauðaR Níu, titled simply “I”, starts with soft tones by two voices. As this one minute piece proceeds, a gentle gong sound and some light percussion are heard; a subtle and mysterious beginning. “II” sets a completely different tone. A sharp drum rap begins, serving as a starting exclamation point. The two voices weave in and around each other in sustained tones amid much howling and spooky vocals. Another series of bangs from the drum and a woodblock add to the unnerving atmosphere. “III” returns to a more settled and soothing feeling. A low sustained vocal in one voice is made more expressive by the light tinkling of chimes. Very mystical and solemn with lovely vocals and reverential sentiment. “IV” continues in a sacred feeling, opening with an Ahhh sound in a single voice. Another voice joins in, accompanied by quiet gong tones and a low drone. The exotic – almost Asian – feel of this is supported by devout vocals, gentle chimes and percussion. “V” continues in the exotic groove and returns to the more forward style with drum raps and sharp woodblock beats. The voices seeming to chant with out words but in eerie, sustained tones. There is a decidedly spectral and anxious feeling to this. “VI” returns to the more subdued refinement heard in “IV”, with a soft opening and chimes. A sudden drum strike with wood block recalls the mood in “II”. A gong is heard between the sustained and almost mournful vocals. There is a sacred, worshipful feel to this. “VII” continues with chimes and a high, plaintive opening vocal. The top voice soars in very high, airy sweeps. More chimes accompany. The excellent singing, heard in very high registers, is controlled, on pitch and does not lose its power. “VIII” opens with a strong drum strike and woodblock rap. Loud, almost screaming vocals are heard, as if in great surprise. A palpable sense of danger and fear is present. Loud drum and woodblock strikes accompanied by long, descending sweeps of vocals paint a convincing musical portrait of fear and despair, This sets the stage for the final section, “IX” which opens with a haunting vocal solo , soon joined by the second voice in call and response. The voices are subdued with somber descending pitches and accompanied by drum strikes, chimes and gong strikes. All elements of the various sections seemingly combine into a sense of acceptance and fateful resignation. Beautiful, expressive singing is heard as the vocals fade to the finish. With NauðaR Níu, Jeffrey Holmes has forged a vibrant musical connection between the Old Norse culture and our own.The next work on the album is a collection of five short pieces titled Two Walking (1994) by French composer Pascal Dusapin. The text for Two Walking is by American writer Gertrude Stein and the work was originally conceived by Dusapin as a study for his chamber opera To Be Sung. The opening piece of Dusapin’s collection, titled “I. How many little wings” begins with a single lyrical voice followed closely be a second vocal, almost as an echo. Now the higher voice soars in a sustained upward arc with text following in both voices. The vocals bounce and dance around each other, evoking birdlike acrobatics on the wing. As the tempo increases the text becomes louder and more frenetic. A sudden slowing towards the finish provides the listener with a soft landing. “ II. Kiss my lips” begins with a quiet clicking and two voices in a sort of conversation. There is a whispering and intimate feel to this, sung as if in secret. “III. May, June” opens with a long solo note followed by the second voice entering slightly below in a counter melody. Now the notes in each voice volley back and forth effectively. As the text moves faster, crisply sung in short, quick phrases, the result is a pleasingly complex texture that does not sacrifice the beautiful harmonies. “IV. A scene in singing” has both voices starting together but soon singing separate lines. Short snappy phrases are heard in places and at times the harmony is unusual, but the overall effect is both lovely and abstract. The final piece in the Dusapin work is “ V. It seems to be”. Two voices in lower register open in syncopated rhythms and the separate vocal lines produce an engaging, crunchy texture. The pitches and harmony are controlled and balanced, even with the lively phrasing. “ V. It seems to be” is a fine finish to an intriguing work. The concluding work on the album is Melisande (2022), by Marti Epstein, the longest piece at almost 13 minutes. Inspired by the Debussy opera, Epstein re-imagines the story as if told through Melisande’s own experience, rather than as a reflection of others. In this interpretation, “the two sopranos alternate between extending and finishing each other’s words, functioning as a single unit, or singing passages with overlapping, contrapuntal lines that give way to moments of ecstatic release.” Melisande opens with two sustained voices in a delicate harmony and dynamics that vary intriguingly. The vocals become more active, with independent lines weaving in and around each other in a call and response pattern. By 4:10 the voices are singing in common phrases in an effective contrast to the opening. The upper voice is especially impressive, exhibiting a fine tone with strength and confidence. By 7:10 the vocals are in solid harmony and declarative text sung expressively in middle registers. The lines diverge and become occasionally independent, one often following the other. The duet singing here is especially disciplined and precise. At a slowing of the tempo, Melisande fades quietly to its finish. An excellent performance of technically challenging music.New Music for Two Voices is a dazzling exploration of vocal virtuosity that sets – and meets – a very high standard. Hopefully this premiere album by Susan Narucki and Kirsten Ashley Wiest will be the first of more to follow. New Music for Two Voices is available in digital download or CD format from: Bandcamp:HB Direct: The post Susan Narucki & Kirsten Ashley Wiest – New Music for Two Voices appeared first on Sequenza21.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录六首当代无伴奏声乐作品，由两位女高音Susan Narucki与Kirsten Ashley Wiest合作演绎，其中三首为世界首录。整张专辑完全去除了器乐伴奏，迫使两位歌唱家完全依赖内在的节奏感与音准默契。首曲为荷兰作曲家Rozalie Hirs的come sempre（2025），意大利语歌词，两个声部独立编织，在不断变化的调性中形成绵密和声，技术难度递增但始终控制精准。哥伦比亚作曲家Alba Potes的TRINOS则受诗人Javier Tafur González启发，由Narucki于2024年委约，包含十二首不到一分钟的声乐小品，每首捕捉特定瞬间——抒情、怀旧、欢腾或希望，精致如宝石般闪烁。专辑附有详尽的解说文字、全文翻译及作曲家和演奏者介绍，录音工程由Andrew Munsey与Kristina Tran完成。整体聚焦于当代声乐技巧的前沿探索，呈现纯人声的可能性。

items.body: Review by Deadwing — Terrifying angels is PRR 4th album after their comeback, with another fantastic release! (4th in arow if you ask me!)They are back to a heavier sound, after the softer and more reflective Coming Up to Consciousness.Still, there are a lot of new experimentations, and it is their proggiest album in the discography,especially due to the 2 larger tracks. The production/mixing was done by Bruce Soord which is shownin a beautiful and balanced composition: the guitars sound heavy but also very crispy with tightsounding and the drums are beautiful and probably the best mix in their discography.All the trademark elements of PRR are here: Heavy and groovy guitars, very grunge and industrialsounding, distorted soundscapes, eletronic passages and multi-layared vocals.Standout tracks are Black-Arrow Acrobats and Hold Your Wrath, featuring unexpected turns, ambience,creative chord progressions and build ups. Spin Like Fire and Haywire Heart are explosive rockingstandout singles. Rumination Ruin is an excellent companion to the sublime title track and BelowRadiance is a more electronic piece with a beautiful composition and ambience.
items._cn_summary: 这是PRR重组后的第四张专辑，在风格上从前作较为内省的氛围回归更厚重的吉他音色，同时融入更多实验性元素，被认为是其最具前卫摇滚特质的一张作品。制作由Bruce Soord完成，吉他音色兼具重量感与清晰度，鼓的混音在乐队历史上堪称最佳。作品中保留了乐队标志性元素：厚重律动的吉他、grunge与工业质感的声音设计、失真音景、电子段落以及多层人声。专辑包含两首长篇曲目，突出特点是意外的转折、氛围铺陈和富有创意的和声进行。单曲如《Spin Like Fire》和《Haywire Heart》展现了爆发力，《Below Radiance》则偏向电子化，呈现出更具空间感的器乐编排。整体在传统前卫摇滚框架内大胆引入工业与电子元素，适合喜欢跨界融合的听众。

items.body: There was a useful logic to the running order of Friday night’s show at Klub Łącznik. Antibody, Agonoize and System Noire all make music designed to work physically, but they approach that physicality from quite different directions. Antibody built movement through rhythm and the almost compulsive momentum of hard electronic dance music. Agonoize converted it into confrontation, theatrical violence and direct exchange between performer and crowd. System Noire then expanded the same basic principle into something broader and increasingly combustible, combining electronic force with the dynamics of a full band. The evening became an accumulation of different ways of controlling a room. The concert was part of the 2026 run pairing Agonoize with System Noire, with Antibody as special guest; for System Noire, the tour also marks the Hanover band’s 10th anniversary. The Wrocław date was officially scheduled at Klub Łącznik, the concert space within Czasoprzestrzeń at the former Dąbie tram depot. Antibody Photos: Karo Kratochwil Antibody opened the evening, and first a small correction worth making because the name is easily mangled: the project is the work of Jan Laustroer. Laustroer began Antibody in 2013, when he was only twelve, and over the following years developed a sound drawing on industrial, power noise, dark electro and the harder end of rave and hardcore. The debut album Opera of Death appeared in 2017, while the more recent Never Quite Right was released in 2024. In January this year Antibody also collaborated with Grendel on “The Ranidae.” What worked especially well in Wrocław was that none of this required the opening slot to pretend it was already the climax of the night. Antibody’s set was extremely danceable, rhythmically insistent and immediately mobile. The tracks worked through repetition, sharp changes of pressure and bass strong enough to make the body respond before there was much reason to analyse what was happening. It was energetic without becoming shapeless; Jan understands that hard electronic music needs more than volume and speed if it is supposed to sustain movement. The visual presentation supported that. Against a star-filled background, the recurring frogs added a deliberately absurd signature to a set otherwise built around hard, mechanical momentum. They have become an immediately recognisable part of Antibody’s visual vocabulary, and after this year’s Grendel collaboration The Ranidae, their presence felt even more appropriate. There was something rather charming about the collision: pounding industrial rhythm underneath, a small amphibian mythology unfolding behind it. As an opener, Antibody did exactly what was needed. The set did not simply “warm up” the audience in the conventional sense; it established movement as the evening’s basic mode of communication. By the time it ended, the room was no longer waiting for the main acts. Agonoize Photos: Karo Kratochwil The change was immediately visible when Agonoize came on. The space in front of the stage became noticeably denser, bodies moved closer together, and the kind of dancing established during Antibody’s set turned into something more collective and more aggressive. Agonoize were formed in Berlin in 2002 and have spent more than two decades making the relationship between harsh electronic music and extreme stage performance central to their identity. Their current touring page explicitly designated the Wrocław concert as a “Blutshow”, continuing the use of theatrical blood that has long been part of the band’s live language. Their most recent full studio album remains Revelation Six Six Sick, released through RepoRecords in April 2021. Calling what happened at Łącznik simply “brutal” would miss why the set worked. The force was carefully organised. The electronics were dense, abrasive and extremely physical, but they also retained enough rhythmic definition for the material to still work as dance music. Chris L.’s performance depends heavily on this ambiguity: he confronts the audience while simultaneously demanding its participation. And participate they did. The stage blood is obviously theatrical, but the reaction it produces is real. Chris repeatedly showered the front of the audience with it, leaving faces and clothes streaked red, and the people closest to the stage seemed delighted to become part of the spectacle. The distinction is important. Agonoize’s blood show does not function particularly well when treated as something happening to a passive crowd. In Wrocław it became reciprocal. People moved forward knowing very well what was coming. They danced harder, reached towards the stage and quite visibly enjoyed being pulled inside the performance. That made the visual violence feel less like decoration attached to the songs and more like an extension of their physical logic. Chris’s gestures were large and confrontational because the music required a body capable of matching its exaggeration. The show continually crossed the line between concert and grotesque theatre without allowing the theatrical element to weaken the musical one. The encore shifted the visual vocabulary again. Chris returned wearing wings, and after so much aggression, blood and pressure, the image had a surprisingly different weight. It was beautiful precisely because the evening had not prepared us for beauty in any conventional form. The wings did not suddenly turn the performance sentimental; they introduced another register into a stage language that had spent most of the set emphasising impact and provocation. My conversation with Chris afterwards changed how I thought about the performance even further. We had previously discussed his long absence following a very serious illness, but hearing him describe the extent of the recovery in person gave that history a different scale. He spoke about having to rebuild abilities that most people never consciously think about, including basic everyday tasks and forms of recognition, through an exhausting rehabilitation process. I would not want to turn illness into an inspirational narrative imposed on the concert, because that would reduce both the person and the performance. But it does change the meaning of what one has just witnessed. Returning to a stage is one thing. Returning to this kind of stage presence, where the performance demands constant physical engagement, vocal force, timing, theatrical control and the ability to command a densely packed room, is something else. The striking thing was not simply that Chris was back. It was the absence of caution in the performance. In our recent interview, he told me that he has nothing to prove to anyone except himself and that what he wants, fundamentally, is simply to continue making music. Watching this set, that statement became much less abstract. The stamina was visible, certainly, but more important was the appetite behind it. This did not look like someone tentatively reclaiming an old position. It looked like someone fully inhabiting it again. System Noire Photos: Karo Kratochwil If Agonoize generated the evening’s most theatrical violence, System Noire converted the accumulated energy into something broader and, by the end, almost unruly. The Hanover project was founded in 2016 and is celebrating its tenth anniversary this year. Its current formation has grown beyond the original electronic core, and the band’s recent material increasingly allows guitars and a harder industrial-metal edge to interfere with its dark-electro and EBM foundations. Their 2024 album Aftermath includes ten tracks and was followed in February 2025 by Lost Control, whose single version the band themselves describe as harder and more guitar-driven, while a separate club edit strips it back towards electronics. That tension between programmed precision and a more volatile live-band attack was exactly what made the final set work. By this stage the audience no longer needed persuading. Smoke filled the stage, the lighting became much more aggressive, and the room that Antibody had initially taught to move and Agonoize had pushed into increasingly physical participation now had very little reserve left. System Noire used that. Their music has enough melodic architecture to keep the songs readable even when the performance becomes extremely dense. That mattered here. The combination of electronics, forceful vocals, percussion and the heavier edges of the current sound could easily have collapsed into undifferentiated volume; instead, the rhythmic centre remained very clear. People could dance to it. The lighting and smoke also worked unusually well with that construction. They were not merely there to make the stage appear “dark”. Smoke repeatedly altered what could actually be seen: musicians emerged, disappeared and reappeared as the lights cut through it, creating a visual equivalent of the music’s own alternation between defined melodic lines and heavier blocks of sound. And gradually the whole thing became wonderfully disorderly. By the final part of the set, the dancefloor was no longer behaving like a room of individuals politely occupying their allotted space. Movement propagated through it. People were dancing hard, responding to the band and to one another, and the distinction between observing the show and physically participating in it had largely disappeared. Calling it carnage is not much of an exaggeration, although it was an exceptionally friendly form of carnage. System Noire therefore made sense as the final band, even though Agonoize might initially appear the more obvious dramatic climax. Their set did not need to out-provoke what had come before it. Instead, it took the accumulated kinetic energy of the entire evening and gave it somewhere to go. Klub Łącznik Photos: Karo Kratochwil Klub Łącznik itself deserves some credit for why the evening felt so comfortable despite the intensity inside. The venue sits within Czasoprzestrzeń at the former Dąbie tram depot, and its layout provides something particularly useful for this kind of scene event: a clear separation between the physical density of the concert hall and the open area outside. Inside, there is a proper concrete-floored club space where a hard-electronic show can become as loud, smoky and physically crowded as it needs to be. Outside, the yard changes the social rhythm completely. Between sets people could step out, cool down, talk, meet friends and, importantly, encounter the musicians without the strange separation that larger venues often create between audience and performers. That mattered more than it might sound. A night involving three relentlessly physical electronic sets can become exhausting when there is nowhere for the intensity to dissipate. At Łącznik, it could. The outside conversations, pauses and meetings with the bands gave the evening breathing space, while every return indoors felt like deliberately re-entering the pressure. Three approaches, one increasingly crowded dancefloor What I liked most was that the evening had progression without needing an artificial concept imposed on it afterwards. Antibody made the body move through rhythmic precision and rave-derived momentum. Agonoize turned the same physical response into confrontation, participation and grotesque theatre. System Noire then took an audience already pushed far beyond passive listening and drove that energy through the dynamics of a full, forceful live set. The crowd grew thicker, sweatier and considerably bloodier as the night progressed, but the atmosphere never became hostile. Quite the opposite. There was a great deal of warmth underneath the noise: people dancing, talking outside, meeting musicians, returning inside and throwing themselves back into it. And perhaps that is the detail worth keeping. With music this aggressive, the obvious vocabulary is always brutality, darkness, violence and impact. All of those things were present. What made the Wrocław show successful, however, was how much pleasure there was inside that aggression. Antibody looked playful behind the pounding rhythms and wandering frogs. Agonoize turned theatrical bloodshed into something the front rows actively wanted to share. System Noire finished with smoke, light and enough accumulated movement to make the floor feel barely contained. By the end, Klub Łącznik looked appropriately wrecked, and the people inside it looked extremely happy. About Agonoize, System Noire and Antibody Agonoize formed in Berlin in 2002 around vocalist Chris L. and have built more than two decades of work around harsh electronic music paired with extreme, theatrically violent stage shows. Their most recent full studio album, “Revelation Six Six Sick,” was released through RepoRecords in April 2021; Side-Line marked that release with a streaming concert announcement at the time. Earlier releases include the 2019 EP “Blutgruppe Jesus (-) / Schmerzpervers 2.0” and the album “Midget Vampire Porn.” Ahead of the Wrocław date, Side-Line interviewed Chris L. about returning to the stage after a serious illness and new material. System Noire, from Hanover, were founded in 2016 and marked their tenth anniversary in 2026. Side-Line first profiled the project in a 2017 Face The Beat feature. The band’s sound has expanded from its original electronic base to include guitars and a heavier industrial-metal edge, documented on the 2024 album “Aftermath” and the February 2025 single “Lost Control.” Antibody is the project of Jan Laustroer, who began releasing music under the name in 2013 at the age of twelve. Side-Line introduced Antibody in a 2016 Face The Beat profile and later featured the track “Secrets” as a 2019 free download. Laustroer’s debut album, “Opera of Death,” followed in 2017, with “Never Quite Right” arriving in 2024. In January 2026, Antibody collaborated with Grendel on “The Ranidae.” Agonoize, System Noire and Antibody played Klub Łącznik, the concert venue inside the Czasoprzestrzeń cultural centre at Wrocław’s former Dąbie tram depot, on September 25, 2026.
items._cn_summary: 这是2026年Wrocław一场演出的现场乐评，三支乐队Antibody、Agonoize与System Noire依次登台，呈现出对舞池控制力的不同策略。Antibody作为开场，以硬电子舞曲的节奏驱动和压迫性低音构建身体动员，视觉上以青蛙元素搭配星空背景形成荒诞与机械感的碰撞。Agonoize将这种动力学推向对峙与剧场化暴力，强调表演者与观众之间的直接能量交换。System Noire则将基本原理扩展为更具爆炸性的全编制乐队动态，融合电子力量与现场乐器张力。文章以现场调度与身体反应为核心观察线索，详细记录了每位艺术家的舞台表现、背景信息及巡演脉络，文字扎实且具备乐评深度。

items.body: John Coltrane – The John Coltrane Quartet Plays (Impulse, 1965) By Dan Sorrells Most of my listening hours are spent on freely improvised music. But when it comes to Coltrane, I love the classic quartet, 1965, right before things broke open (and the group, apart). The John Coltrane Quartet Plays is what I reach for most often. “Chim Chim Cheree” starts like another “My Favorite Things,” but less than a minute in, Coltrane’s already chafing against the melody, and after two he and Jones are fairly bursting out of Tyner’s measured vamp. “Brazilia” and “Nature Boy” enticingly point toward the searching explorations to come, where ideas were turned inside-out in dizzying, kaleidoscopic epics (something further evidenced by various surfaced recordings from the Half Note during the same period, where “Chim” and “Song of Praise” stretch to twice the length). The sense that traditional song forms must still be made to contain Trane’s increasingly frenetic probing lends indelible tension to the music; these songs are like swelling water ballons, but they’re filled with boiling water. For those of us in the future, it’s all the more heightened when you know just how far things will get pushed, even before the close of the year. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张1965年Impulse唱片将Coltrane四重奏推向自由爵士的临界点。专辑从迪士尼曲目"Chim Chim Cheree"切入，起初类似"My Favorite Things"的东方调式循环，但不到一分钟Coltrane便开始挣脱旋律束缚，与鼓手Elvin Jones共同从McCoy Tyner的节制和声背景中迸发而出。"Brazilia"和"Nature Boy"以短小篇幅预示了此后更为深邃的探索方向，传统歌曲形式被作为容器，盛放日益狂热的即兴探询与张力，专辑整体呈现出暴风雨前夕的高度紧绷感，对于了解Coltrane年末彻底转向自由爵士的听众而言，这种张力因预知结局而被进一步放大。乐评以亲历者口吻指出该作是其最常回听的Coltrane录音。

items._cn_summary: Acousmatic Crossings 系列由 Metapsychosis 主办，本期呈现两部声音作品。Andrew Czink 的《Iron Emerald》（2005）探讨声音之间的关系如何暗示超越其可识别声源的事物，属于典型的声学音乐（acousmatic music）创作，关注声音本体的抽象感知。Zazie Productions 的《Spectral Ode to Synesthesia》（2025）则以脉冲噪声、拾得物、现场录音等多元素构建空间性作品，并涉足联觉这一感官交叉主题。两位艺术家均来自实验音乐领域，关注声音的物质性与空间感。该系列聚焦于当代电声音乐与声音艺术的交叉地带，适合对纯粹聆听体验与声音设计感兴趣的听众。文章内容偏短，仅为片段摘录，信息深度有限，但所涉及的作品方向与实验/电声音乐领域高度契合。
