items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Drone music is nothing new of course having existed in ancient musical forms ranging from ancientHindustani and Carnatic styles to Japanese gagaku, Byzantine chants and Scottish bagpipes however interms of more modern Western music it really got a foothold in the early world of electronic musicwhen La Monte Young began a new minimalist experimentalism that has continued to the current day. Bythe late 60s acts like Finland's The Sperm and Germany's Kluster soon to be Cluster as well aslesser known artists like Italy's Harry Bertoia were really warming up to the possibilities of darkambient sounds set to a sustained note. A handful of acts began to follow suit however oneinteresting artifact from the early 70s was the album PLANES by the duo of GREGOR C�RTEN & ANSEMROGMANS who only entered the musical arena to record this sole album before C�RTEN would move on tothe world of visual art and painting while ROGMANS would become a school teacher and choir director.For having no prior history and no future releases, PLANES is a surprisingly cool album that fitright into the burgeoning progressive electronic and Krautrock sweeping the German music scene ofthe era. This album came out in 1974 and featured two sprawling tracks that each swallowed up anentire side of the vinyl release. Following in the footsteps of Kluster, Eliane Radigue and La MonteYoung, GREGOR C�RTEN & ANSEM ROGMANS crafted a haunting display of electronically hypnotic dronefreakiness that seemed to be part Kluster, part early Klaus Schulze and part A.R. & Machines. Whiledrone music is hit and miss with most acts missing the mark of what it takes to deliver attentionkeeping minimalism that can sustain an album's worth of material, PLANES is an interesting rarityfrom the era that offers a nice escapist's paradise into a sonic playground that finds just enoughspices to keep it all enthralling.The first side simply titled "Planes I" sounds like a musical shaving session with a buzzing soundthat sounds like an electric razor that establishes itself a good while before haunting wordlessvocalizations and creepy organs find themselves embellished by a series of random electronic effectsand tape manipulations. While the droning effects are in the forefront, the tenebrous organ riffsand lugubrious vocals are quite chilling as the track slowly drifts through its 18-minute plusduration. The contemplative buzzing mediation adds that certain uneasiness while the pacifyingpredictability simultaneously soothes the soul. The second track titled "Planes II" offers a totallydifferent spin albeit in a similarly themed droning drift that also lasts just slightly longer thanthe 18-minute mark. This one opens with a tinny repetitious guitar twang that slowly changes pitchup and down the scale and then joined in by a slow monotonous organ drone that also incrementallyflows glacially. This particular effect is very much out of the Achim Reichel playbook but yetsounds totally unique in this context. Drone music can be quite dull if not done properly but these guys really knew how to generate analbum's worth of exhilarating drone music by creating a fascinating slow building tension that couldhave been one of the inspirations of the later post-rock. The album artfully incorporates the tonesand flavors of progressive electronic, especially the Berlin School variety along with Krautrocktechniques only funneled into a more minimalist drone style of slowly unfolding musical innovations.The production is very good and the album is best experienced loud and on a good speaker where youcan feel the reversing micro-changes of the pitches which offer an entire body experience. It's aninteresting underground relic of Germany's fertile musical underground and one that shouldn't bemissed by lover's of electronic escapist music. While Kluster is the most brandished reference, thismusic isn't nearly as bleak and industrial sounding and more detached in a creepy drugged outexperience way.
items._genre: drone / progressive electronic / dark ambient / krautrock
items._cn_summary: 1974年德国二人组Gregor Cürten与Anselm Rogmans的唯一专辑《Planes》由两首各占唱片一面的超长曲目构成，将电子嗡鸣、管风琴低鸣与人声采样交织于持续音之上。第一面以电动剃须刀般的持续嗡响开场，辅以阴森的无词人声与管风琴变奏，在十八分钟的绵延中制造不安与安抚并存的聆听体验；第二面以单调变化的电吉他拨弦与缓慢漂移的管风琴持续音展开，呈现冰川式流动的冥想质感。该作品可视为Kluster、Klaus Schulze早期及La Monte Young传统的延续，将极简主义持续音美学与德式前卫电子场景相融合，录音仅此一次，成员随后转向视觉艺术与教育领域，使这张专辑成为早期暗氛围与德国实验电子发展史中一份罕见的孤本。

items.body: Review by Stroumpf — Imbued with post metal and symphonic movements cores of death, black and abstract math metal fuse in a Large Orgone Collider -a showcase of overpowering inventiveness and technical bravuraStephen Jarrett's despondent, hyper-agile, 'psychological' guitar narrates and nervously navigates the manic, fluctuating surreal world of external horrors it builds: a landscape of dread and overwhelming doom textures to simulate a complete eclipse. As sonic, technically overpowering dramaturge, master-narrator and litterateur withing the distinct sub-genre of abstract tech metal, he shares an astonishing conceptual and technical lineage with Robert Fripp and Steve Hackett.With a melancholy anthropomorphic elephant holding a mandolin on the album cover (and who does not know that African forest elephants disperse the seeds of the ebony trees from which premium guitar fingerboards are made), one is likely to think of a surreal Jazz festival poster. 'Jazzy' and surreal in an abstract tech death metal way, linear through-composed the ride is going to be, starting with an instrumental accelerando that could be an after-thought to The Goliath's 'Vomited Hyacinths'. The album asserts its individuality with the titular second track 'Joyless Parson' which forms together with the razor-sharp Slayer-esque head cleaner 'Mourn' (an instant classic of furious beastliness) and the monolithic 'The Void of course' (Voc) -a non-formulaic center piece and multi-movement epic- the three pillars of this piece of avant-guard art.With the analytical prose-anti-poetry telling us about the wretched and tortured joyless parson, who is kept alive by a contemptuous life force, his pastoral illusions ('fantastic lies worth repeating' up until his 'feeling unworthy of pleasure [?] guarding alone a cache of treasure which no one values and no one visits'), there seems not much space for emotional growth: nevertheless, the musical representation of a hypnotic decent into human depravity and existential paralysis offers us a breath-taking juxtaposition of intense mathematical dissonance and serene, sorrowful classical melodicism and haunting chamber melancholy (piano and cello) prefiguring their 2024 masterwork 'Pleroma'. Abandon expectations of genre-typical, traditional metal anthems with refrains along a uniform hyper-fast blast beats-driven grid (though Orgone can do anthemic, world-shattering riffs and head-banging stuff, too). The guitar work (and the guitar does all the work) centers on non-repeating distinct upper register micro-phrases -shall we call them micro-riffs or 'micro-memes?'-, each bar organically and erratically mutating into the next. The ever-shape-shifting guitar work will mimic and impressively dramatize how a hapless individual racks his brain. Layers of Black Sabbath DNA lie bare: knotty, sludgy riffage, almost minimalistic, primitive playing style and muddy mid-range crunch make appearances. But it's Tony Iommi on amphetamines: everything is shot through, imbued and augmented with expressive, breathtakingly inertia-free fretboard swash-buckling, rapid-fire interval leaps, chaotic chromatic shifts, attacking pushing micro-timing driving the beast, counter-melodic playing and harsh dissonances. Jarrett's anti-traditional soloing is existential protagonist, agitator, catalyst and jumpingly associative propellant. Beside itself in a mental flow, it is its own antagonist, commenting, probing, cajoling, shooting distracting flares; it falters and picks itself up again, flays the strings, wields justice on the hoof, runs evasive maneuvers, inserts evocative moments of respite and serenity expanding with soaring climaxes of staggering beauty (again and non-repetitively again). The guitar work literally whips and drags the band along, until heights of despair turn into blazing technical and melodical fireworks.'Void of course', an astrological term apparently refers to the moon's transitioning between Zodiac signs and its running into emptiness symbolizes a time of [self-imposed] isolation. The 14 min long song serves as the album's emotional and sonic anchor. Much of JP's runtime is therefore spent in sinuous, drifting fluctuations, patient, lumbering builds, a suffocating crawl forming heavy, expansive doom and echoey post metal atmospheres before straight-ahead aggression strikes again up to successions of disorienting peripeties, drawn-out climaxes and releases, culminating in some grotesque dance of the near-dead and a very painfully evocative, psychotic Caspar Br�tzmann-like pingy, plinky-ploink disintegration fest. A heart-breaking atmospheric drop into a mental chasm follows with a shuddersome coda. Most guitarists would have exhausted and repeated their vocabulary of tricks and phrases several songs ago. Multi-instrumentalist and ego-free gentleman shredder Jarrett, however, up to the messy, slightly fuzzy, synoptic round-up track 'Circulated Treason' that even contains slivers of uplifting, playful music, he just keeps on giving. As the architect of its own nightmare, he layers chaotic, multi-tracked arpeggios that are like structural fractures. Drummer Justin Wharton utilizes staccato shifts, sudden stops and accelerations to sound out the psychological load with servings of disorienting time-signatures and something akin to American Primitivism while (even) the deft vocal delivery adds vocal percussion, atmosphere and inimitable lyrical heft.'Joyless Parson' is bleaker, more doom-laden and was recorded only 1 year after its equally inspired, very, very fast predecessor 'The Goliath'. The slowing down allows breathing space for the instruments and incredible skills to shine. Together they stand closer to the brain-frying, punishing mathcore debut 'Accumulator' than to the multi-voiced, genre-fluid, maximalist super production 'Pleroma' [2024] though the idioms, and symphonic sweep are already manifest.Oh well, the album lacks a bit of sound engineering clarity (especially compared to the follow-up 'Pleroma') -but so what? Hey, we know what it is meant to sound like and that's all that matters! An utterly uncompromising 96%

items._cn_summary: ORGONE 的《The Joyless Parson》将后金属、死亡金属与抽象数学金属熔于一炉，吉他手 Stephen Jarrett 以高度非重复性的高音区微乐句作为叙事核心，持续有机变形以具象化人物的精神挣扎。专辑以线性通谱写法构建，配合钢琴与大提琴等室内乐元素，在数学性极端不和谐与古典哀歌之间形成对比。三首核心曲目——同名曲、Slayer 式强力和弦猛作《Mourn》及多乐章史诗《The Void》——撑起整张前卫艺术框架。黑安息日泥泞 riff 是其根骨，但在 Iommi 式的极简上叠加了技术狂躁，使整张作品在极端金属框架内呈现出鲜明的实验性与文学性叙事意图，预示了乐队后续 2024 年作品的方向。

items.body: Da Punch is the fourth album from the Parisian project Krystal System. ‘Bonnie’ and ‘N°7’ are joined by a new member, bassist ‘Phi’, who had already appeared on the EP preceding the album. Remarkably, this is their first full-length release since 2013. On ‘Da Punch’, Krystal System takes a critical look at society and interpersonal relationships, resulting in a collection of 13 tracks. I’ve always had a soft spot for Krystal System because, to me, they sound like a big ‘f*** you’ to all those bands that simply keep repeating themselves, gradually getting lost in a lack of creativity. Krystal System continues along its established path, delivering uncompromising compositions that blend guitar and electronics into an Electro-Post-Punk sound, driven by Bonnie’s passionate vocals. She sometimes sings in her native French, but most of the tracks are performed in English, delivered with that unmistakable and rather sexy French accent. N°7 also takes the microphone, providing a nice counterbalance to the female vocals and occasionally resulting in a duet. The songs are varied and, as mentioned, uncompromising. Their cover of Front 242’s “Headhunter” is a great example. Rather than simply copying the original—which would be sacrilege—they give it their own interpretation, and it really works. There are other, even stronger tracks to discover, with Krystal System occasionally channelling Rammstein-like guitar riffs and Depeche Mode-style melodies, while still remaining firmly rooted in their own sound. That’s what I call a modern Punk attitude, and it really appeals to me. Krystal System will need to put themselves back on the map for a wider audience, but music lovers who already know the band will simply be delighted to see them return with such a cool album. (Rating:8). Listen to “A World That Is Yours”: A World That Is Yours by Krystal System About Krystal System Krystal System started in Paris, France, in April 2006 under the name Krystal. The founding duo was Bonnie on vocals and guitar and N°7 (also stylized as Seven) on vocals, synths, and programming. A first demo, “Demain n’existe pas,” came before the project gained early exposure through the 2007 International Cravefest Video Awards and concerts in France and Switzerland. Around 2007 the duo signed to Belgian label Alfa Matrix and adopted the name Krystal System. Their debut album, “Underground,” followed on November 14, 2008, then the seven-track EP “Underground: VooDoo Night Sessions” on November 27, 2009, “Nuclear” on June 17, 2011, and “Rage” on March 15, 2013. Krystal System returned in 2025 with the “Éclats Rouges” EP, its first studio release since “Rage” and its first with bassist φ (Phi), expanding the lineup to a trio. “Da Punch,” the fourth Krystal System album, followed on June 26, 2026, again with the trio of Bonnie, N°7, and Phi. The 13-track release was made available digitally via Bandcamp and on CD through the Alfa Matrix Store, whose edition adds two bonus tracks, “Newclear Winter” and a 2025 version of the track. The album also includes a cover of a Front 242 song, “Headhunter.”
items._cn_summary: Krystal System 第四张专辑《Da Punch》由巴黎三人阵容完成，贝斯手 Phi 加入后，吉他与电子声响进一步交融。主唱 Bonnie 以法式英语呈现，N°7 则以男性声线形成对位与重唱。十三首作品延续乐队对社会的批判视角，在不妥协的编曲中融入 Rammstein 式吉他切分与 Depeche Mode 式旋律线条，同时保持自身辨识度。对 Front 242《Headhunter》的重新诠释并非简单复刻，而是将原作结构拆解后以电气化手法重构，保留了原作冷峻气质并注入新的张力。专辑发行于比利时独立厂牌 Alfa Matrix，CD 版额外收录两首 bonus 曲目。乐评整体肯定其在类型框架内的持续探索与拒绝重复的态度，认为对于熟悉乐队的听众而言，这是一次令人满意的回归。

items.body: Documenting Sound is a new tape and digital series from Boomkat Editions. Over time, they will release a number of recordings from a selection of artists, all from different parts of the globe and a wide range of musical disciplines. These pieces, made during the last couple of pandemic-hit months, offer a personal and intimate glimpse into the artist and their music. The only condition was that the music should be recorded at home or in its own surroundings, without too much in the way of pre-planning or thoughts surrounding its composition. As a result, the music is open and unexpected, going outside the box and wandering far, making this a series perfect for artistic exploration. Instead of presenting an impoverished viewpoint of lockdown, the pandemic has resulted in a creative explosion as artists and musicians livestream and record from home. Field recordings, found sounds, improvisation, spoken word, and song-writing were all encouraged, and this edition, entitled Gathers, features an hour of new music from Sarah Davachi, recorded at her home in Los Angeles in Spring 2020. ‘I’ve been going through various stages of movement – some days I can’t be motivated to do anything and other days I can spend long hours working on music and going deep into it. When I’ve been able to sit with making music, it’s been incredibly meaningful and reconfiguring for me at this moment. I’m thankful to have the time in my studio, a room that is calm and quiet and feels quite distant from the outside world, and this cassette is essentially a reflection of that interiorized state of being.’ ‘Gathers’ has grown out of two separate ideas and albums – one completed but as-yet-unreleased, and another currently in development. The improvised and unedited cassette can take the listener somewhere else even while they stay at home, becoming lost in the music, and Gathers feels both meditative and focused. The A side brings together harpsichord, harmonium, and piano. Sarah describes her harpsichord as being ‘my main instrument these past few weeks…these Renaissance tunings have such depth, a house of endless hallways, and it’s been great solace to disappear into them temporarily.’ These past few months have also disappeared, the strangely shaped and hazy afternoons erasing, time spooling as spring turns into summer, but they’ve also allowed connections to grow once again – connections and roots that have been severed or at least cut back by the demands of everyday life. The downtime has, perhaps, resulted in greater flexibility, opening introverted thoughts as people adjust to a more sedate way of life. In this recording, time is slipping; the quarantined music is the sound of a lie-in and a day that drags, but it also sounds focused, running deep. A session can become a deep-dive, and one can remain immersed for hours at a time. My synthesizers are like old friends. They were my first passion when I started collecting instruments, and this period of time has been a nice excuse to revisit some of them. Side B collects three electronic studies for Mellotron, electric organ, and synthesizer, which is combined with tape echo. Sarah describes them as her…’chosen electronic instruments, and the ones through which I’ve always found the highest degrees of stillness and transformation’. And that’s what this lockdown has done: not only a pause, but a cocoon in which a transformation has taken place, and from which the music has finally emerged, taking its first flight into a new and changed world. www.boomkat.com
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Boomkat Editions新系列的一部分，邀请音乐人在疫情期间居家录制，强调即兴与非预设的创作方式。Sarah Davachi在洛杉矶的家中完成了约一小时的作品，将大键琴、簧风琴与钢琴的声音层叠融合，营造出沉静绵延的氛围。她形容大键琴的文艺复兴调律如同一座无尽的走廊迷宫，带来深刻的慰藉。整张磁带没有经过剪辑与编排，是内省状态的直接映射。音乐呈现出时间感模糊、缓慢拉伸的质感，听者可以完全沉浸其中数小时。评论将这段居家录音视为封锁期间创造力爆发的例证，强调安静的创作环境如何孕育出聚焦而冥想式的聆听体验。

items.body: Blood Transmission is Dag Rosenqvist’s first solo album in three years. Welcome back! This is Dag in a thoughtful frame of mind; the notes are as sparse as an empty room, missing extravagant embellishments save for the necessary furniture. Everything is in order, uncluttered, highly organised, as if the music had suffered a visit from Marie Kondo and her never-ending checklist. Dag’s music does spark joy, but it’s restrained. Things are slow to get going (which is a good thing). A whipping wind jettisons into the atmosphere, freefalling into the track, and jagged, triangular synth-teeth burst up from the bedrock, taking clean bites out of the atmosphere with a nightmarish ferocity to match the shark in Jaws, whose naughty antics plagued the coastal town of Amity all those years ago. The danger is there – often hidden, concealing itself in the lower half of the sea’s horizontal divide – but it’s not shy to rise up and make your acquaintance when it wants to. Notes bubble up from the fathomless deep, and something is always building just beneath the track, the tension festooning around the outskirts of the track like an incoming headache. The pulsating heartbeat doesn’t let up; it keeps pumping and the legs keep on running, draining the battery and recording thousands of steps on its Fitbit. Blood Transmission is all about creating and destroying. Soft piano interludes seep into the cracks, while behemoth synths snap back in a vicious attack. It’s not an immediate threat: it comes at you from angles, with a Hadouken and a side-punch. Before you know it, the track is in the process of munching on aural take-out, a speedy devouring of the atmosphere it had first scented and then tracked and then attacked. Rolling synths avalanche and create an unstoppable force. Penultimate track ‘From Rivers to the Sea’ could have generated from a F*** Buttons album thanks to the heavy thumping of the beat and the electrocuted synth, forming a progression of raw and euphoric power, but quieter waters are never far away. Take the finale, ‘Absolutes’, which lands on a Queen-sized bed made of soft feathers. A piano comes to clean up the synth’s atrocity, daylight clearing away the debris. It’s another moment of renewal in an album that’s peppered with them. The piano is a steady stream, its water flowing like blood and its blood flowing like water. We’re gonna need a bigger boat. Blood Transmission by Dag Rosenqvist www.hiddenvibes.bandcamp.com

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑呈现了极为克制的声响美学，音符稀疏如空荡的房间，合成器锯齿状音色从基底猛然刺穿大气层，形成鲨鱼般潜藏的威胁感。钢琴与巨型合成器交替出现，前者如细流渗入裂缝，后者以残暴姿态撕裂氛围。专辑核心在于创造与毁灭的循环：低音区始终酝酿着紧张与不安，脉冲节拍如同心跳持续驱动张力积累，最终以钢琴清流洗涤合成器的暴行收束。末尾曲目回归柔软的羽毛床，象征废墟上的新生。整体结构缓慢推进，留白与爆发形成鲜明对比，融合暗潮氛围、实验电子与后摇滚的质感，在独立厂牌发行，保持了地下场景的艺术纯粹性。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑聚焦圣多美和普林西比这两个大西洋小岛在七八十年代录制的Puxa舞曲。Puxa融合了葡萄牙语非洲殖民地传统节奏，并混入merengue、Soukouss、Kompas等多种元素，体现了非洲、加勒比与葡语世界的跨洋文化交织。乐评指出，岛屿地理偏僻、录音工业薄弱，使得现存录音更显珍贵。文章重点推荐了Pedro Lima领衔的乐队，其闷哑吉他与鼓手形成激烈对话；Sangazuza则以简约编制展现纯粹律动；Africa Negra的曲目展示了复调人声与缠绕吉他的有机结合。作为Bongo Joe厂牌发行的考古式再版，这批录音将一个鲜为人知的音乐场景首次系统呈现给国际听众，对世界音乐爱好者具有重要参考价值。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了贝宁歌手兼巫毒教实践者Antoine Dougbé在1977至1982年间与Orchestre Poly-Rythmo的合作录音。Dougbé以拍腿演奏Cavacha节奏闻名，该节奏由鼓手Belobi Meridjo从火车节奏中提炼，后蔓延至1970年代中期的刚果流行乐。专辑呈现明显的古巴son风格影响，开场曲目以合成器铺垫，吉他音色带有塑料质感的年代痕迹，高帽主导的律动贯穿全曲，合成器与吉他在行进中交错编织。在Dougbé短暂的三张专辑与零星单曲生涯中，他展现出对乐手演奏契合度的严苛要求，认为Poly-Rythmo能精准实现他的音乐构想。这批录音融合巫毒传统、刚果伦巴与古巴元素，是Analog Africa厂牌对这位被忽视的音乐人的重要梳理，呈现了西非流行乐在七十年代末受多方影响后的独特面貌。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._genre: experimental jazz / Norwegian folk fusion / free improvisation
items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio的最新专辑在前作科幻合成器与民谣素材结合的探索基础上，回归更为脚踏实地的方向，但跨文化寻索的脉络依然延续。主奏乐器为高音萨克斯，爵士影响贯穿始终。首曲改编自挪威西部传统春季舞蹈配乐，乐队以低音提琴和鼓构建节奏骨架，随后叠加模块合成器和颤铁琴丰富色彩。乐评特别强调三人的角色分配从不固定，乐器之间的旋律与节奏功能持续流动互换，从主题呈示逐步过渡到即兴展开，高音萨克斯在尾声再次回收旋律形成收束。这种打破常规编配逻辑的弹性结构，以及将挪威民俗素材融入爵士即兴语汇的手法，体现了乐队一以贯之的实验态度。整体篇幅较短，仅对开篇一首曲目进行了较为详细的技术描述，但已足以展示其融合策略与即兴理念。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家奥马尔·索萨在意大利法齐奥利音乐厅完成了一场两小时无脚本的独奏即兴，录音后通过稀疏地加入人声片段、打击乐、循环、田野录音与拾得音效进行后期混音。评论聚焦于艺术家对'风格'的有意回避——他将爵士、拉丁、古典等元素融汇成新的整体，而非归于任何既有类别。专辑诞生于疫情封锁与个人转折期，索萨将其视为一段内在旅程的记录。录音在空旷音乐厅中以三角钢琴为核心，'少即是多'的美学贯穿始终，后期点缀的极简配器保留了原始即兴的自发质感。评论包含艺术家本人对流媒体算法与市场分类的反思，以及对自由聆听群体的描述。

items.excerpt: Just when Steve Reich’s ninetieth birthday celebrations appeared to be drifting towards an inauspicious conclusion, along comes Charles Hazlewood and the Paraorchestra to gatecrash the party, tear up the rulebook, let loose a posse of Dionysian dancers on the scene, and transform a routine Reich event into a Bacchanalian rave. items.body: Just when Steve Reich’s ninetieth birthday celebrations appeared to be drifting towards an inauspicious conclusion, along comes Charles Hazlewood and the Paraorchestra to gatecrash the party, tear up the rulebook, let loose a posse of Dionysian dancers on the scene, and transform a routine Reich event into a Bacchanalian rave. This new take on Music for 18 Musicians provided a breath of fresh air amongst a raft of retrospective events—Reich remodelled and refracted through the prism of psychedelia and 1990s warehouse EDM, with perhaps a whiff of hippy idealism and transcendental meditation thrown in. I’m not sure whether the composer would have approved. Most of those present gleefully lapped it all up. Hazlewood is known for thinking creatively outside the box, but here he appeared to be operating according to a completely different set of Euclidean principles. To be sure, Reich’s music has been placed in a variety of unorthodox settings and spaces over the years, ranging from disused train station buildings and repurposed multistorey car parks to all manner of outdoor locations, so there was nothing inherently radical in presenting this classic work at Southbank Centre’s Clore Ballroom. Nevertheless, dotting the ensemble around the space went against Reich’s own recommended set-up, as did Hazlewood’s encouragement for everyone to move about the space as if viewing an audible sculpture in an art gallery. Likewise, the idea of dancers moving in and around the ensemble was not in itself revolutionary. Reich’s music, including Music for 18, has provided accompaniment to several dance productions in the past, notably those of Laura Dean Dancers and Musicians, and Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker’s Rosas dance company. However, the idea of interpolating freestyle, improvised movement seemed to fly in the face of the piece’s austerely conceptual pretext. Hazlewood rightly drew attention, in a brief announcement at the beginning of the evening, to a whole range of paradoxes that lie at the heart of Reich’s music—not least that between rigor and freedom—and it was certainly refreshing to see Music for 18 unfettered from its structuralist straitjacket. There’s certainly nothing wrong with shaking things up, so long as the intention is motivated by creative and artistic concerns rather than dramatic effect. While there’s no doubting that Hazlewood’s intentions were genuine, the results were not always persuasive. The dance element, pre-planned beforehand, tended to shift attention from the sonic experience to a visual one, and while the idea of encouraging the audience to move in and around the space was in keeping with Music for 18’s ‘immersive’ impact, this too became something of a distraction. Many members of the audience appeared to circumambulate the space in a kind of somnambulistic daze, and the whole point of the exercise—to listen more attentively to the music—seemed to go by the wayside. I can’t imagine for a moment that walking around while trying to avoid bumping into other people doing the same thing might in any way sharpen one’s focus on the complex layers and textures that underpin Reich’s groundbreaking work. Thankfully, most seemed to have had enough of moving around after the opening set of eleven pulsing chords. So much for walking as a gradual process. I remained firmly anchored to the vibraphone station—the composition’s ‘signal box’ and timekeeper—where the rest of the ensemble could be heard in more-or-less perfect balance. What seemed to get lost in all the theatrical paraphernalia was the music itself, which was a shame since the Paraorchestra’s performance was never less than impressive, and at times quite brilliant. Highlights included brightly hued, bell-like clarinet and vocal buildups in Sections II, IV and IX; surging tonic-dominant movement in the pianos in Section IIIa; warmly glowing and flowing marimba and vocal colours halfway through Section V; and excellent ensemble coordination in Section X. And despite my cautious reservations about the happening-style multimedia nature of the performance, Sections VI–VIII, with their infectious maracas groove, yielded an extraordinarily uplifting synergy between music, dance and movement. At that moment, the entire performance clicked into place. As an experiment, this presentation of Music for 18 certainly possesses potential, but perhaps it’s worth taking a closer look at those early, gritty, grungy performances of minimalist music in New York’s large lofts and gallery spaces during the late 1960s and early ’70s. Photos of these early performances show audiences scattered about the venue, as was the case here, but sitting (or lying down) on cushions rather than walking around, with an amplified ensemble positioned at the centre of the room. Perhaps future audiences should be encouraged instead to bring a beanbag, lie back, and let the music wash over them, wave after beautiful wave… The post Steve Reich at 90: ‘Music for 18 Musicians’ (The Clore Ballroom, Southbank Centre, London, 27 September 2026) appeared first on Sequenza21.
items._cn_summary: 为庆祝Steve Reich九十岁生日，指挥Charles Hazlewood与Paraorchestra在南岸中心Clore Ballroom重新演绎了经典作品《Music for 18 Musicians》。此次演出打破了Reich原有的空间布局，将演奏者散布于场地各处，并加入自由即兴的舞者穿梭其间，融入迷幻舞曲与90年代仓库锐舞的美学元素。乐评指出，Hazlewood试图揭示Reich音乐中严谨与自由之间的悖论，将作品从结构主义束缚中解放出来。尽管意图真诚，实际效果却不尽人意：舞蹈元素预设的编排使注意力从听觉转向视觉，观众在场内漫游的行为反而干扰了对音乐的专注聆听。整体演出在创意构思上颇具胆识，但在艺术说服力上存在落差，是一次带有实验野心的再诠释。

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Solaris by The Ocean is a great step forward for the German sludgy atmospheric prog metallers, allowing new vocalists Enrico Tiberi & Lane Shi great room to show off their unique talents. Musically more epic since their Phanerozoic album series, it sees the band create longer compositions that gives great drama and atmosphere. While I was a massive fan of former vocalist L�ic Rossetti, Tiberi's cleans and barks are a perfect replacement, adding the same drama and emotion but with his own unique flair, while Shi's unique chants and screams are an extra dimension to the bands sound, which adds an almost creepy mood to the thick atmosphere the band create. The use of industrial electronic noises throughout are also great at adding mood to the overall pieces. I'd give this a mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Belligerence.

items._cn_summary: 德国乐队The Ocean的新专辑Solaris被评论者视为乐队自Phanerozoic系列以来的重要进步。新主唱Enrico Tiberi的清声与嘶吼兼具，承担起戏剧性与情感张力，Lane Shi的吟唱与尖叫则为乐队厚重的氛围增添了近乎诡异的色彩。音乐上延续了乐队擅长的氛围化处理，作品篇幅更长，叙事与戏剧性更强，工业化电子噪音作为氛围铺底的元素贯穿整体结构，营造出浓郁的沉浸感。评论者给出8分评价，并推荐曲目Belligerence作为切入点。该专辑融合了金属乐的重量感与实验性氛围塑造，工业电子元素的加入拓展了传统后金属的边界。

items.body: Hey friends, quick update from the Senior Staff on the eve of the spooky season. It’s been real busy for us in both in non-IDUD related life stuff, and as such it’s very possible we are overlooking new records and artists that we should have our eye on. Thus it’s time for a renewal of our annual plea to please, tell us what we haven’t covered that you think would be to our taste. You can do it right here in the comments of this very post? As much as we enjoy a good dig through Bandcamp and various setlists from respected DJs and friends, we’d love a blindspot check from our readers, who have generally never steered us wrong with that sort of thing. We’d sure appreciate it. Seven Trees Mesh, “Trying to Save You” Bristol’s Mesh are such a unique quantity in the big umbrella that is Our Thing. Taking synthpop and rendering them with rock band energy isn’t the easiest move in music, but they’ve always pulled it off with aplomb. See new single “Trying to Save You” from the forthcoming mini-album “Fallen Angel” for example; big hooks, bold arrangement choices (that switch up as it exits the chorus is so clever) and lots of momentum. Truly no other band sounds like them. Fallen Angel by Mesh Aurat, “XIII” Coming just a few months after the dense and spiky Cobra EP, this teaser from Aurat’s forthcoming silhouette LP portends something quite different from the highly touted and fast moving LA act. Forsaking their EBM tendencies, this cut carries their goth/post-punk genome into unexpected doomgaze territory. Is it reflective of the whole release? We’ll be sure to follow up in a month’s time. silhouette by Aurat Kontravoid, “Chances” Kontravoid is no stranger to writing a great electro-pop jam; you could probably build a decent mixtape out of cuts from across the catalogue like “Too Deep”, “Losing Game” and “Faceless”. Strong possibility you’d throw “Chances”, another taste of the upcoming Sound of the Void to that list also, it’s exactly the kind of catchy, danceable, melancholic but forceful cut that Cam Findlay has been casually knocking out for some time now. We wouldn’t be shocked to hear this at any given goth club or darkwave party over the next couple of years, it’s fun and spooky in the right ways. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Chalice Sect, “Silent Fever” Chalice Sect is a new name to us but it doesn’t take long to cotton onto the LA act’s rhythmically pummelling read on darkwave on this track from their forthcoming Finis Initii EP. A slew of heavily distorted synths which sound as though they have more in common with the aggro side of synthwave than goth drives things further into a maximalist space which will likely irritate purists but probably goes off live quite well. Finis Initii by Chalice Sect Nasdrowie, “Impact” Shout-out to friend Nick for bringing this EP from Nadrowie to our attention. It’s largely instrumental, but the vocals on “Impact” position it as the sort of murky 90s electro industrial that is like candy to us. Raw and rough, you could hear this being spun in a set with any number of classic Zoth bands. For fans of Evil’s Toy, and maybe Seven Trees? A New World To Cry by Nasdrowie Seven Trees, “Underneath My Skin” Speak of the devil, here’s a pleasantly moody and stark new cut from the aforementioned reactivated Swedish dark electro vets Seven Trees. As with their 2021 comeback LP Dead/End “Underneath My Skin” isn’t trying to leap off the page at you, but as the simple but solid structure beneath the clean and icy programming rolls along, the track progressively builds a sense of dread and inevitability that leaves a lasting chill. Solid and considered stuff for those who prioritize mood and affect in their dark electro. Underneath My Skin by Seven Trees The post Tracks: September 27th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评以专栏形式介绍了多支暗潮及电子音乐人的新作。Mesh将合成器流行乐以摇滚乐队能量重新演绎，单曲钩子鲜明、编曲转折巧妙。Aurat在最新单曲中舍弃了以往的EBM倾向，转向带有末日凝视气质的后朋克与哥特融合，展示了音乐方向的新探索。Kontravoid延续其标志性的忧郁电子流行路线，旋律上口且适合舞池。Chalice Sect则是新面孔，以高度失真的合成器堆叠出最大化、带有侵略性的暗潮声响，可能引起纯粹主义者不满但现场效果强劲。整体侧重于类型内部的单曲推荐与口味推荐，信息密度适中。

items.body: Mexico City producer Dimitri Berzerk released his second full-length album, “Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo” (“As on Earth, So in Heaven”), on September 24, 2026, through his own label, Sector Industrial Producciones (SIP). The eleven-track record blends synthpop and industrial elements in a style Berzerk calls “Esoteric Body Music.” He built the release as a concept album accompanied by a printed book, with illustrations by Amanda Lunares. The label’s own description characterizes the album as music “seeking to illuminate the dark paths within us and help us rediscover what has been lost.” Berzerk describes Esoteric Body Music as the balance point between synthpop and industrial, tied to concepts drawn from philosophy, alchemy, astrology, and sacred geometry. Tracklist and credits for ‘Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo’ The album has eleven tracks: “Inevitabilis,” “Surgere,” “Statera,” “Solvere,” “Syzygia,” “Intemerata,” “Coniunctio,” “Coagulatio,” “Concordia,” “Cadere,” and “Insanabilis.” Berzerk wrote, composed and recorded the songs in Mexico City between 2024 and 2025, except “Cadere,” co-written with Mexican musician Hari Sama in 2024. Traditional Hindu texts appear on “Inevitabilis.” Fragments on “Surgere,” “Statera,” “Intemerata,” “Concordia” and “Cadere” come from “The Book of Tokens” by Paul Foster Case. Sergio García and Quetzalcoatl Gutiérrez mixed and mastered the album in Dolby Atmos at Studio Quetzalcoatl in Mexico City. Berzerk designed the album concept and the accompanying book himself; Amanda Lunares created the artwork and illustrations. Guest vocalists include Pedro Dabdoub on “Inevitabilis,” Pedro Gopar of Prismatic Shapes on “Surgere,” Pascal Languirand of Trans-X on “Statera,” Amanda Lunares on “Solvere,” Heka on “Syzygia,” Montse Magia on “Intemerata,” and Norms Dom on “Coniunctio.” Additional musicians include Chuz Estrada on drums (“Inevitabilis,” “Statera”), Guillermo Torres on guitar (“Surgere”), Raul García on guitar (“Cadere”), Helena Sánchez Soto on vocal arrangements (“Insanabilis”), and Adrián Díaz Hilton on choir arrangements (“Insanabilis”). Gustavo Cid recorded voice on “Coniunctio”; Moises Navarro recorded voice on “Intemerata” and “Insanabilis.” A concept album with an accompanying book “Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo” is built as a concept album. The book that accompanies it uses Amanda Lunares’ illustrations as symbols tied to the album’s themes. SIP states the album explores emotion and perception together, continuing the philosophical and esoteric direction of Berzerk’s earlier work. Physical CD-and-book edition planned SIP states a physical edition is coming, in a CD-and-book package, following the same approach used on Berzerk’s previous album. His 2023 debut full-length, “Nineteen Eighty-Four,” was also released in book format, according to the Mexican outlet Casete.com.mx. No release date, order link, or pricing for the physical edition of “Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo” has been confirmed. Where to hear ‘Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo’ The album streams and is available to download on Bandcamp. SIP’s promotional material describes the album as available “across all music platforms,” but as of publication the album could not be found on Spotify or Apple Music, where several of Berzerk’s earlier releases, including “Nineteen Eighty-Four” and “The Liquid Path,” are listed. Wider platform availability for the new album is unconfirmed. About Dimitri Berzerk Dimitri Berzerk is the recording name of Dimitri Loyo, a DJ, producer, remixer and label owner based in Mexico City. He told Side-Line in a 2021 interview that the name “Berzerk” draws on the Atari video game of the same name, his first exposure to vocoders, and on the Norwegian band Apoptygma Berzerk, an act he likes. The two are unrelated projects. Berzerk began DJing in 2005, performing at nightclubs, festivals and on radio across Mexico, with more than a thousand performances across the Americas and northern Europe, according to Casete.com.mx. From 2009 he produced remixes under the alias DMT Berzerk, releasing more than a hundred of them, including eight remix compilation volumes issued on physical formats through Conzoom Records (Germany) and Subterrane Records (Australia), both now out of print. Under his own name, Berzerk founded Sector Industrial Producciones and released three EPs on the label by mid-2021. SIP also issued “Remixes Collection Vol.02” (May 2018) and “Remixes Collection Vol.03” on CD (October 2018), both reviewed on Side-Line. From 2019 he began releasing original material under the Dimitri Berzerk name, with eight singles and EPs issued on CD, vinyl and digital through Norwegian label Sub Culture Records. In November 2022, he became a third member of Mexican act C-Lekktor, alongside Markko and Jamie. Berzerk released his debut full-length album, “Nineteen Eighty-Four,” on March 3, 2023, compiling and reworking tracks from his earlier EPs with guest vocalists including Claus Larsen. Side-Line’s review called it a blend of “danceable electro-pop with harder EBM songs” and rated it 8/10. Casete.com.mx reported the album was also presented in book format. Berzerk followed it with the “Resist” EP in October 2024, released via SIP in digital, CD and vinyl formats, again featuring Claus Larsen on guest vocals. “Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo,” released September 24, 2026, is Berzerk’s second full-length album and continues the concept-album-and-book format he used on “Nineteen Eighty-Four.”

items.body:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.

items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?

items._cn_summary: 这是丹麦三人组合GuldGanger的首张数字EP，由北欧民谣界资深歌手Mia Guldhammer领衔。五首曲目大多基于传统民谣素材，乐手们各自融入不同的演奏视角。开场曲《Svennedal》节奏粗粝奔放，充分展现了她富有说服力的嗓音；唯一的原创曲目《Nordgård》由乐队成员Morten Musicus创作，口琴与风笛带来强劲的推进感。《Agnete Of Bjergmanden》中，扬琴营造出细腻的音色背景，口琴与乐器交织出富有弹性的层次；终曲《Orms》作为纯器乐曲，长笛与弦乐融合出一种奇特的不稳定张力。整张作品呈现出古朴而粗粝的氛围，乐队虽为新组建但已显得相当成熟。

items.body: Psalm 68 says Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to Elohim, one of the Hebrew Bible’s names for God, and Rastafari read the verse as prophecy, fulfilled when Haile Selassie I took the Ethiopian throne in 1930. Julian Asher, a reggae singer from Cape Town now living in Berlin, paraphrased it in the notes to his debut EP, Haile Abeba Sound, and on “Elohim” he builds a whole song around the name. He sings of a He and a She arriving at full strength to reclaim an ancient throne from those who lead people astray, and calls on Abba and Selassie I by name across the verses. The music comes from Downtown Steppas, a Berlin backing band who also build their own riddims. The partnership goes back to “Perilous” in 2022, and “Just Cause”, a single Asher cut over the band’s Fantasia riddim, now shares its name with their first album together. Just Cause was recorded last winter, from songs singer and band had been playing together for years. Stream “Elohim” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Julian Asher & Downtown Steppas – Elohim appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由开普敦出身、现居柏林的雷鬼歌手Julian Asher与柏林伴奏乐队Downtown Steppas合作完成，融合拉斯塔法里精神信仰与雷鬼节奏。专辑曲目源自双方多年来的现场积累，去年冬季正式录制完成。歌曲以希伯来圣经《诗篇》第六十八篇为文本基础，围绕Elohim这一神之名展开叙事，呼唤Haile Selassie I，描绘古老王权的回归与拯救。乐队自建riddim伴奏体系，使作品在传统雷鬼框架内保持制作独立性。从风格定位来看，此作属于雷鬼/世界音乐范畴，与用户偏好的实验前卫、学院派爵士、电子实验及暗潮方向存在一定距离，但在跨地域文化融合（南非与柏林）与拉斯塔法里精神主题方面具备一定文化深度。

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — To Keep the flame alive, to know how to rekindle it when needed. To show perseverance and courage to face difficulties, tragedies, absences, and times that aren't always favorable?standing tall, against all odds, despite the captain's age. These are the qualities Vittorio Nocenzi had to bring together to resurrect Banco Del Mutuo Soccorso in the 2010s, to pull it back from the darkness where so many of our illusions were lost, and to bring to fruition the surprising *Transiberiana* in 2019, followed by *Orlando, la forma dell'amore*, the second album by the band's new lineup, that is to say, without Gianni, who has been pursuing a solo career since the '80s, and without Giacomo or Rodolfo, who departed without a trace for the highest heavens, the realm of the musical geniuses of our time. It's hard not to draw a parallel with PFM, another legendary figure of the Italian progressive rock scene during the "imperial decade." For both bands, we've witnessed a splendid comeback after a period?long or short?of inactivity, creative stagnation, or even alarming setbacks (the mid-1980s), a return to the forefront of the prog scene led by a founding member (Franz Di Cioccio for PFM), a shared desire to return to more ambitious compositions mixed with more straightforward ones, and a shared ability to surround themselves with new, highly talented musician friends and lyricists, as well as a young recruit who brings a certain sense of the spirit of the times (Vittorio's son from Banco and Luca Zabbini of Barock Project, who contributed keyboards and composition to more than half of PFM's latest album). The result is a similar musical style: smooth symphonic prog blended with vigorous jazz-rock. Without wanting to pit them against each other, I tended to give a slight edge to PFM's latest album (I Dreamed of Electric Sheep) as Zabbini's talent as a composer sometimes makes all the difference. But Banco's unbridled romanticism, magnified by an exceptional new singer (the impressive Tony D'Alessio), may give it greater and more lasting appeal. With the help of his son Michaelangelo and lyricist Paolo Lugli, Vittorio Nocenzi presents *Orlando*, an ambitious and highly compelling concept album, both for its subject matter (inspired by the famous chivalric poem *Orlando Furioso*, composed in the early 16th century by Ludovico Ariosto?known as "l'Arioste"?as a sequel to Matteo Maria Boiardo's *Orlando Innamorato*) and for its generous running time (nearly 80 minutes, the equivalent of a double album from the vinyl era) and the form it takes (progressive instrumentals straight out of the '70s, an 11-minute epic, a refreshing diversity?), as well as by its determination to return to the roots of RPI right from the start of the record (the formidable "Proemio"/"La Pianura Rossa" sequence). With melodies that hit the mark, a rich use of keyboards featuring dizzying Moog solos, nods to the past, sparkling rhythms, and harmonic inventiveness that rarely falters, *Orlando* seems to follow in the musical footsteps of its predecessor, while going a step further on the path back to its roots, bringing us all those poignant memories that are more like scents than thoughts. As you listen more and more, you quickly forget the few moments that are a bit saccharine ("L'Amore Accade"), dull ones ("Serve Orlando Adesso"), incongruous ones (the bandoneon tango in "Non Mi Spaventa Pi� L'amore"), or even questionable ones (the overly conventional blues of "Non Credere Alla Luna")?and instead focus on the remaining 60 minutes, a level of quality rarely achieved by Banco since the late '70s, with a few major highlights such as "Le Anime Deserte Del Mondo" (The Deserted Souls of the World?what a beautiful title!), where the best of Banco's golden age comes together for five divine minutes with Kate Bush (on bass), Keith Emerson (on repetitive piano), PFM, and Battiato. A delicate harmony emerges from this unlikely blend, as if the graceful notes in this track were passing through a mysterious filter. "L'isola Felice" is another irresistible moment, bewildering with its Caribbean-style intro, xylophone, and subtle electronic backdrop, its monotone yet edgy vocals, and its unexpected Hammond organ solo. But for the listener, this track is indeed all about bliss and rapture. Some may prefer "Cadere O Volare," which the band premiered in a video a few months ago and which is described as "the perfect musical synthesis of this album, a perfect example of the variety of arrangements," ranging from a classical string quartet intro to the electric guitar of the best jerky Italian pop of the '80s, and culminating in a '60s-style Hammond organ solo after passing through a quiet, acoustic interlude. Yet another resounding success. Added to the two instrumentals?which are hard to resist?we have here five little gems of modern Italian pop that shine so brightly they manage to outshine the lengthy "Moon Suite" (11:49), which is by no means without merit. Memorable above all for its first section?in the purest, dynamic Banco style?and for the melodic finesse of its second section, this highly anticipated long progressive suite generally lives up to its promise. Despite a few weaknesses and its length, *Orlando, le forme dell'amore* comes closest to what one would expect from a fascinating Banco?a band capable of blending the sound and spirit of contemporary melodic rock with a more traditional transalpine prog without being stuck in the past, and capable of transporting you to another dimension. After more than 50 years, Banco remains a living legend, bringing the tale of Sir Roland to life in modern terms and through music embroidered with jazz-prog gold via a rich and generous new album?even if it isn't consistently thrilling or ideally progressive (and vice versa).

items.body: Review by sgtpepper — The first APP album has captured hearts of many progressive and pop enthusiasts.It sounded contemporary, even futuristic (vocal vocoder) with the clean, imaginative production and the great concept selection with the another Al(l)an, Edgar Alan Poe.In comparison to the later albums, music is not that radio friendly yet and music keeps being ambitious and focused, where the duel among vocalists vs instrumentals are pretty levelled.The band shows knack for emotional ballads ("The Cask of Amontillado", "To one in paradise") which will be perfected on other albums. I have always liked the symbiose of emotional music, great studio talent (no surprise when speaking of Alan Parsons) and curious instrumentals. The flagship of all APP instrumentals is presented on the second side of the album "The fall of the house of Usher". It comprises 5 parts, all of them both progressive and symphonic without any playing excesses.No wonder this album belongs to the highest acclaimed APP albums and carved a unique blend of styles on the European music map.

items._cn_summary: 这是The Alan Parsons Project首张专辑，以美国作家爱伦·坡的文学作品为概念蓝本，串联起多首叙事性曲目。制作人Alan Parsons展现出精湛的录音室技艺，运用了声码器等在当时颇具未来感的音色处理手段，赋予作品干净的声场质感。器乐与声乐之间保持着均衡的对话关系，抒情段落已展现出对情感氛围的塑造能力，但相比后期作品更具实验野心。第二面的器乐组曲分五个部分展开，在交响化与前卫化之间游走，避免了炫技式的冗余演奏。整张专辑将文学概念、流行旋律与前卫编制熔于一炉，在欧洲乐坛树立了独特的混合风格坐标。
